abstract: "Checking whether published articles archive usable data and code is time-consuming: even the lightest form of computational reproducibility checking, running an article's own code on its own shared data, has been estimated to take around 24 minutes per article, and writing independent analysis code from scratch has been estimated at 2-25 person-hours per article. Cooper and the BES Data and Code Hackathon Group (2026) manually coded data- and code-archiving practices in 1861 papers published across the seven British Ecological Society (BES) journals between 2017 and 2024, using a two-day hackathon of 145 participants who followed a bespoke coding protocol. This manual effort is exactly the kind of task that automated tools such as Metacheck aim to support: extracting structured information about open science practices from the text and repositories linked to a scientific article, in a fraction of the time. We ran Metacheck's `repo_check`, `data_check`, and `code_check` modules on the same corpus and compared its output against Cooper et al.'s human-coded ground truth for every construct where a direct, mechanical comparison is possible: data availability, archive location, data licensing, data and code download success, code archiving, and README presence. For each construct we report sensitivity, specificity, and two directional miss rates (how often a human coder caught something the tool missed, and vice versa), and, going beyond aggregate accuracy, we individually reviewed every disagreeing paper against Metacheck's saved output, the paper's own text, and, where relevant, a live call to the repository platform's own API, to determine which side was correct and why. Agreement on whether data could be downloaded and used was 99.0%, and on whether code could be downloaded was 99.5%; agreement was lower and more variable for whether a repository could be found at all (83.9%), whether code was archived (87.4%), and whether a README was present (71.8%). Metacheck's precision is consistently high across constructs — when it reports a repository, license, download, or README as present, that report is rarely spurious — but its recall is uneven and construct-dependent, driven by a mix of a repository-detection coverage gap (a real, working data or code citation on a platform or in a format Metacheck does not yet recognise), a structural limitation in inspecting the contents of compressed archives, and at least one genuine definitional mismatch (platform-level description metadata a human coder reasonably reads as README-equivalent, which Metacheck's stricter file-presence check does not). Our goal is not to replace manual coding of this kind, but to clarify, concretely and per construct, where automation can currently reduce the burden of large-scale meta-scientific data collection while maintaining comparable accuracy, and where it currently cannot, and why."

## Introduction

The last two decades has seen a notable culture change around open science practices. Universities, journals, and funders increasingly expect researchers to engage in open science practices. One open science practice that has become especially widely required and adopted is data and code sharing. The goal of data and code sharing is to facilitate re-use, and to increase transparency. Funders have started to require data management plans that specify where and how data and code will be made available for re-use, and submission guidelines for journals often require that data and code underlying the claims in a manuscript are shared if possible. The British Ecological Society, for example, requires that "all data and code supporting the results in the paper must be archived in a public repository" (https://www.britishecologicalsociety.org/publications/journals/author-guidelines/).

Although the requirements to share data and code are clear, it is less clear who is responsible to check that authors actually follow through on these requirements. Manually checking data and code files is a time-consuming task that requires expertise about best practices in data and code sharing. Due to the diffusion of responsibility and the lack of resources to check whether scientific manuscripts follow best practices in open science, requirements to share data and code are often not followed, and if data and code are shared, best practices are often not followed. Cooper and the BES Data and Code Hackathon Group [-@cooper2026] assessed data- and code-archiving practices across the seven journals published by the British Ecological Society (BES). They found that most manuscripts in which data was used also shared the data, but code sharing was less common, and even when data and code were shared, best practices were often not followed. About a third of data and/or code repositories lacked a README file, code not always well-annotated, and code was not always reproducible (e.g., due to hard-coded file paths). These findings strongly suggest that it would be beneficial if data and code is reviewed before a manuscript is published.

Some journals manually check data and code before an article is published. This practice is most common in economics journals, where a dedicated Data Editor oversees the reproduction of results based on data and code (@vilhuber_report_2025). Manual checks are laborious and delay the publication process. It is therefore not surprising that researchers are exploring automated ways to check whether data and code are shared, and whether they are usable. For example, the Scalable Infrastructure for Validation of Computational Social Science Research (SIVACOR) pilot project by the data editors of the American Economic Association examines whether it is possible to automatically verify the computational reproducibility of data and code. The extent to which automated processes can reduce the workload associated with checks of data and code sharing practices is an open question. Automation has the potential to reduce the workload of manual checks, but it is not clear whether and where automated tools can achieve the same level of accuracy as human coders. 

In this paper we will examine how Metacheck, a novel open source tool that checks best practices in data and code sharing, might assist in the process of checking whether data and code are shared. We will compare the output of Metacheck against the manually coded ground truth of Cooper et al. [-@cooper2026], available at https://github.com/nhcooper123/reproduce-reuse-recycle, to determine where Metacheck can currently reduce the manual burden of large-scale meta-scientific data collection while maintaining comparable accuracy, and where it currently cannot, and why. It is clear the human coders exerted considerable effort over the 2-day hackathon to code the 1861 papers, where 145 people coded a median of `r median(as.numeric(table(master_comparison$recorder_ID)))` (min = `r min(as.numeric(table(master_comparison$recorder_ID)))`, max = `r max(as.numeric(table(master_comparison$recorder_ID)))`) manuscripts. Cooper et al.'s protocol covered the seven journals published by the British Ecological Society (BES), coding papers published between 2017 and 2024 on eight questions per paper.  The team coded whether data and code were used and archived, where they were archived, whether the archived files could be located, downloaded, and opened, what file formats were used, whether a README was present and how useful it was, how complete the archived data were, how well-annotated the code was, and whether the data and code were citable (i.e., had a DOI and a licence). 

This is precisely the kind of structured, repetitive, and time-consuming coding task that automated tools such as Metacheck [@R-metacheck] aim to support. If an automated tool could complete some or all of Cooper et al.'s eight coding questions at comparable accuracy to their trained human coders, it would substantially reduce the workload that is currently required to check if researchers follow best practices in data and code sharing. Metacheck [@R-metacheck] is a modular, open-source tool that uses text search, rule-based classification, API's, and optional large language models to extract information about research practices from scientific manuscripts and their associated repositories. It contains three modules — `repo_check`, `data_check`, and `code_check`that perform automated checks that closely resemble the questions Cooper et al. [-@cooper2026] asked their human coders to answer.

In this paper, we use Cooper et al.'s openly archived data as ground truth [@cooper2026zenodo], and for each of the eight questions in their protocol, we (1) summarize what Cooper et al. found, quoting their own text verbatim, and (2) examine, concretely and with reference to specific Metacheck module output fields, whether that question can currently be automated, partially automated, or not automated at all. Where automation is possible, we run the relevant Metacheck module(s) on the same 1861 papers and report the results. The results generated by Metacheck are completely automated, do not rely on AI, and can be completely reproduced by re-running the code, without any human input.

Unlike a validation study that reports a single accuracy percentage, our goal here is to make transparent, question by question, exactly where the current version of Metacheck can reduce the manual burden of this kind of meta-scientific data collection, and where it cannot. As an automated tool, Metacheck follows FAIR principles, which state that "all research objects should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable (FAIR) both for machines and for people" [@wilkinson_fair_2016, p. 3]. Human coders can retrieve information that is not accessible by a machine. For example, if authors state that the data is shared as supplementary material, the data is not FAIR, because a machine can't find and access the datafile. Cooper and colleagues did not limit their coding to FAIR data, and as a consequence, Metacheck will always miss some information that human coders found. On the other hand, machines can find some information that human coders miss. For example, the Dryad data repository requires a CC0-1.0 license at deposit for every dataset with no author choice involved, and adds this information to the metadata. Metacheck retrieves this information, but the human coders were unable to locate license information by visually examining the Dryad repository. Throughout this project we will also reflect on practical challenges when developing software that attempts to automatically retrieve FAIR data, and the implications for best practices in data and code sharing.  

## Methods

We obtained the list of paper DOIs, journals, and years directly from the cleaned dataset in the public repository, and downloaded all articles through an R script. All articles were converted to structured text using GROBID 9.0, and converted to Metacheck paper objects. We ran the `repo_check` (locates and lists files in online repositories), `data_check` (classifies files and extracts information about tabular data), and `code_check` (checks R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB code files) modules to mirror to manual coding performed by Cooper and colleagues. Subsequently, we ran the `reproducibility_check` module to illustrate additional benefits of automation.

```{r}
#| label: res_modules
#| eval: FALSE ## Set to TRUE to rerun modules

res_repo_check     <- module_run(bes, "repo_check")
res_data_check     <- module_run(res_repo_check, "data_check", cache = TRUE)
res_code_check     <- module_run(res_data_check, "code_check", cache = TRUE)

save(res_repo_check,     file = "code/01_run_metacheck/res_repo_check.RData")
save(res_data_check,     file = "code/01_run_metacheck/res_data_check.RData")
save(res_code_check,     file = "code/01_run_metacheck/res_code_check.RData")

# After rerunning the three modules above, rebuild the small "slim"
# file the data chunk actually reads (see its own comment for why):
# Rscript code/01_run_metacheck/02_build_manuscript_data_slim.R
```

```{r}
#| label: license-value-check

# Computed from repo_metadata (loaded in the data chunk above, from
# manuscript_data_slim.RData) to check a pattern visible to anyone
# inspecting repo_metadata directly: many Dryad-hosted repositories
# report the identical license string. `license` here is read verbatim
# from each platform's own API response (see mc_data_doi/mc_data_license
# below) -- nothing here
# rewrites or standardises it.
#
# is_dryad_url() reads its prefix list from metacheck's own
# .dryad_doi_prefixes() rather than hardcoding only the single most
# common prefix (10.5061) -- an earlier version of this chunk did exactly
# that and, as a result, miscounted 14 genuine Dryad repositories (real
# datadryad.org deposits under one of Dryad's other institutional DOI
# prefixes, e.g. 10.25338, 10.7291, 10.6078 -- confirmed live, each
# resolves to datadryad.org) as "non-Dryad", which in turn made the
# prose below wrongly claim the CC0-1.0 string "never appears for a
# non-Dryad repository". This is the same multi-prefix detection gap
# Appendix A.6 documents and fixes for repo_check's own Dataverse
# DOI-prefix allowlist and for 03_recreate_cooper_columns.R's platform
# labelling -- this chunk had an independent copy of the same narrow,
# single-prefix bug that neither of those fixes touched, since it lives
# only here in the manuscript's own license-value-check chunk.
rmeta <- repo_metadata
dryad_prefix_pattern <- paste(gsub("\\.", "\\\\.", metacheck:::.dryad_doi_prefixes()), collapse = "|")
is_dryad_url <- function(x) grepl(paste0("datadryad\\.org|(", dryad_prefix_pattern, ")/dryad|doi\\.org/(", dryad_prefix_pattern, ")"), x, ignore.case = TRUE)
cc0_url <- "https://spdx.org/licenses/CC0-1.0.html"
n_dryad_total <- sum(is_dryad_url(rmeta$repo_url))
n_dryad_licensed <- sum(is_dryad_url(rmeta$repo_url) & !is.na(rmeta$license))
n_dryad_cc0 <- sum(rmeta$license %in% cc0_url & is_dryad_url(rmeta$repo_url), na.rm = TRUE)
n_cc0_total <- sum(rmeta$license %in% cc0_url, na.rm = TRUE)
n_nondryad_cc0 <- n_cc0_total - n_dryad_cc0
```

```{r}
#| label: data-code-archiving-counts

# Computed from side_by_side (for the Cooper-side and
# unsupported-repository counts) and structure_slim/code_table_slim
# (for the metacheck-side counts -- both loaded in the data chunk
# above, from manuscript_data_slim.RData), and from the host lists the
# installed metacheck package itself uses to recognise a repository
# platform (metacheck:::.dataverse_hosts(), etc.) -- nothing in this
# chunk is typed by hand.
#
# TODO (open question, not yet resolved): accuracy_summary (OddPub vs.
# open_practices accuracy against Cooper's data_open/code_open) is
# computed by 02_create_comparison_data/03_build_master_comparison.R
# and attached to master_comparison.rds as an R attribute rather than
# as ordinary columns/a separate object. An attribute is easy to lose
# silently (it does not survive an unguarded subset or a naive re-save,
# and does not show up in a plain View()/str() of the data frame's
# columns) -- consider having that script return accuracy_summary as
# its own named list element, or its own small .rds, instead.

n_cooper_data    <- sum(side_by_side$data_availability %in% "Yes")
n_cooper_code    <- sum(side_by_side$code_archived %in% "Yes")
n_cooper_either  <- sum(side_by_side$data_availability %in% "Yes" | side_by_side$code_archived %in% "Yes")

# mc_data_availability's own scope: at least one linked repository with
# at least one file of any type found in the main text.
n_mc_repo_found  <- sum(side_by_side$mc_data_availability, na.rm = TRUE)

# "Contained data"/"contained code": at least one file data_check/
# code_check classified as data/code respectively -- broader than
# mc_data_format's own tabular_usable-only scope, since "contained data"
# in this sentence means any data-classified file, not only a file that
# parsed successfully as a usable table.
papers_with_data <- unique(structure_slim$paper_id[structure_slim$data_type == "data"])
papers_with_code <- unique(code_table_slim$paper_id)
n_mc_data   <- length(papers_with_data)
n_mc_code   <- length(papers_with_code)
n_mc_either <- length(union(papers_with_data, papers_with_code))

# Unique repositories (repo_url) holding at least one data- or
# code-classified file, across the whole corpus.
repo_urls_with_data <- unique(structure_slim$repo_url[structure_slim$data_type == "data"])
repo_urls_with_code <- unique(code_table_slim$repo_url)
n_repos_either <- length(union(repo_urls_with_data, repo_urls_with_code))

# The two DIRECTIONAL disagreement counts between Cooper's coding and
# metacheck's "has data or code" judgement, computed directly from the
# two id sets rather than as a naive difference of their sizes
# (n_cooper_either - n_mc_either is NOT the same as
# length(setdiff(cooper_ids, mc_ids)) whenever mc finds papers cooper
# didn't -- it silently nets the two directions against each other).
cooper_either_ids <- side_by_side$article_id[side_by_side$data_availability %in% "Yes" | side_by_side$code_archived %in% "Yes"]
mc_either_ids <- union(papers_with_data, papers_with_code)
n_cooper_yes_mc_no <- length(setdiff(cooper_either_ids, mc_either_ids))
n_mc_yes_cooper_no <- length(setdiff(mc_either_ids, cooper_either_ids))
n_both_yes_either <- length(intersect(cooper_either_ids, mc_either_ids))
n_either_total_disagree <- n_cooper_yes_mc_no + n_mc_yes_cooper_no

# Of the n_cooper_yes_mc_no papers (Cooper says data/code exists,
# metacheck found none), how many trace to repo_check finding no
# repository at all versus repo_check finding a real repository whose
# files data_check/code_check simply did not classify as data or code
# (an emptier, but not zero, disagreement -- the reverse of "repository
# not detected"). Both counts below are restricted to gap_ids itself
# (the n_cooper_yes_mc_no set), so they are mutually exclusive subsets
# of it and sum to at most n_cooper_yes_mc_no -- confirmed directly:
# repo_check found something for 51 papers corpus-wide where
# data_check/code_check classified nothing, but one of those 51
# (10_1002_2688_8319_12029) has NA for both of Cooper's own
# data_availability/code_archived columns, so Cooper made no "Yes"
# judgement to disagree with at all and it is correctly excluded here.
a6_cats_ids_check <- read.csv("code/03_comparing_results/repo_not_detected_categorization.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
a6_cats_ids_check <- unique(a6_cats_ids_check$article_id)
gap_ids <- setdiff(cooper_either_ids, mc_either_ids)
n_repo_not_found_of_gap <- sum(gap_ids %in% a6_cats_ids_check)
n_repo_found_but_no_data_or_code <- sum(
  gap_ids %in% side_by_side$article_id[side_by_side$mc_data_availability %in% TRUE]
)

# n_mc_no_repo_corpus_wide is EVERY paper repo_check found nothing for,
# out of the full 1861-paper corpus, regardless of what Cooper coded --
# this is NOT the same number as n_mc_missed_reviewed (267 as of the
# current repo_not_detected_categorization.csv, computed further below),
# which is restricted to the subset of those "found nothing" papers that
# were ALSO a disagreement with Cooper (i.e. Cooper coded that paper as
# having data or code). Confirmed directly: every one of the current 267
# rows in the categorization file is a Cooper=Yes disagreement (0 are
# Cooper=No agreements) -- the remaining n_mc_no_repo_corpus_wide - 267
# papers are cases where repo_check found nothing AND Cooper agreed there
# was nothing to find, so they were correctly never disagreements and
# never entered the categorization file at all. (This file's row count
# has changed more than once over the course of this project as further
# fixes and rechecks were applied -- re-verify this count directly
# against the CSV rather than trusting a number written here, since this
# comment itself went stale once already.)
#
# The categorization file was cleaned once (2026-09-29) to remove 38
# rows that had gone stale: they described a "repository not detected"
# state from before this session's metacheck platform fixes (4TU,
# Dataverse DOI-prefix, Dryad, Figshare, DSpace7, DataOne) were rerun,
# but repo_check now genuinely finds a repository for all 38 --
# confirmed directly against current mc_data_availability for every row
# in the file, not just the ones already known to be affected. A random
# sample of the remaining rows was independently spot-checked against
# the current repo_check$table output and found to still accurately
# describe "repo_check finds nothing" for each one.
n_mc_no_repo_corpus_wide <- sum(!side_by_side$mc_data_availability, na.rm = TRUE)

# Unique repositories reachable through metacheck's shared-API backends
# (Dataverse, DSpace 7, DSpace 6/legacy, DataOne, Figshare), each
# individually confirmed against a real host rather than guessed from a
# generic pattern, plus its dedicated single-platform integrations.
# n_dedicated_platforms counts each distinct _links()-style detector
# function in the vendored source (code/data/reproducibility_check/vendor/
# metacheck/R/archive-*.R) that recognizes and queries one specific
# platform: 4TU, AsPredicted, Dryad, FSD, GitHub, GitLab, Mendeley Data,
# OSF, ResearchBox, ReShare, and Zenodo (11 platforms). This deliberately
# excludes archive-local.R (local files, not a repository platform) and
# archive-zenodo-upload.R (an upload helper, not a detection integration),
# and excludes PsychArchives, whose host (www.psycharchives.org) is one of
# the DSpace-legacy hosts counted in n_dspace_legacy_hosts below rather
# than a separate dedicated integration.
n_dataverse_hosts <- length(union(metacheck:::.dataverse_hosts(), names(metacheck:::.dataverse_doi_prefix_hosts())))
n_dspace7_hosts   <- length(metacheck:::.dspace7_hosts())
n_dspace_legacy_hosts <- length(metacheck:::.dspace_legacy_hosts())
n_dataone_hosts   <- length(metacheck:::.dataone_hosts())
n_figshare_hosts  <- length(union(metacheck:::.figshare_vanity_hosts(), names(metacheck:::.figshare_doi_prefix_hosts())))
n_dedicated_platforms <- 11L
n_unique_repos <- n_dataverse_hosts + n_dspace7_hosts + n_dspace_legacy_hosts + n_dataone_hosts + n_figshare_hosts + n_dedicated_platforms

# Papers whose ONLY Cooper-coded data_archive value(s) fall outside
# metacheck's supported-platform categories (Cooper's own "Other
# repo/database" catch-all, or "Personal website"/"Supplementary
# materials", neither of which is an externally checkable repository at
# all) -- and, of those, how many metacheck's repo_check consequently
# found nothing at all for.
unsupported_labels <- c("Other repo/database", "Personal website", "Supplementary materials")
is_unsupported_only <- !is.na(side_by_side$data_archive) &
  vapply(strsplit(side_by_side$data_archive, ";"),
         function(v) all(trimws(v) %in% unsupported_labels), logical(1))
n_unsupported_repo <- sum(is_unsupported_only)
n_unsupported_repo_and_mc_missed <- sum(is_unsupported_only & !side_by_side$mc_data_availability, na.rm = TRUE)

# Three-way breakdown of those n_unsupported_repo papers by Cooper's own
# data_archive label. "Personal website" and "Supplementary materials"
# are not FAIR by this paper's own definition regardless of what
# metacheck supports (a machine cannot reliably find/access data at an
# arbitrary URL or embedded in the article's own supplementary file).
# "Other repo/database" is Cooper's catch-all label and is NOT the same
# thing as "a repository metacheck genuinely does not support" -- her
# coders used it for any repository outside their own named platform
# list, which includes real OSF/Dryad/Figshare/Zenodo deposits their
# coding scheme simply had no more specific box for, and metacheck
# supports every one of those. A subset uses more than one of these
# labels together (e.g. "Supplementary materials;Other repo/database"),
# so the two counts below do not sum to n_unsupported_repo.
split_labels <- strsplit(side_by_side$data_archive[is_unsupported_only], ";")
n_unsupported_personal_web <- sum(vapply(split_labels, function(v) "Personal website" %in% trimws(v), logical(1)))
n_unsupported_supp_mat     <- sum(vapply(split_labels, function(v) "Supplementary materials" %in% trimws(v), logical(1)))

# 03_comparing_results/repo_not_detected_categorization.csv (see A.6's own
# fuller loading comment below, where it is reused as a6_cats) is the
# only place in this project a repository's platform was actually
# verified one paper at a time (reading the paper's own text and, where
# relevant, querying the cited platform's own API) -- rather than
# inferred from Cooper's own coded label the way the Other-repo/database
# count above was. UNSUPPORTED_REPO is that verified count: a paper whose
# individually-checked citation genuinely names a platform metacheck has
# no backend for at all, as opposed to a real OSF/Dryad/Zenodo/Figshare
# repository that only *looked* unsupported because of how Cooper's
# coders labelled it, or a paper metacheck simply failed to detect for
# an unrelated reason (a truncated DOI, an embargo, a text-extraction
# artefact -- see A.6's own category table).
a6_cats_preview <- read.csv("code/03_comparing_results/repo_not_detected_categorization.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
a6_cats_preview <- a6_cats_preview[!duplicated(a6_cats_preview$article_id), ]
n_genuinely_unsupported <- length(unique(a6_cats_preview$article_id[a6_cats_preview$category == "UNSUPPORTED_REPO"]))

# Breakdown of the hard, repo_check-outcome-based count -- every paper
# with at least one "repository not detected" disagreement (the same
# population Table 1 below summarises; a6_cats_preview here is the
# identical CSV Table 1's own a6_cats loads later, read once more here so
# this earlier reconciling paragraph has it available). This replaces an
# earlier version of this paragraph that was anchored to
# n_unsupported_repo (a softer count built only from Cooper's own
# data_archive label text -- a paper counted if EVERY label she gave it
# was "Other repo/database"/"Personal website"/"Supplementary
# materials" -- which said nothing about what repo_check actually did
# and, being label-based rather than outcome-based, never summed to
# Table 1's own total). nrow(a6_cats_preview) IS Table 1's total.
n_mc_missed_reviewed <- nrow(a6_cats_preview)
n_mc_missed_unsupported_repo <- sum(a6_cats_preview$category == "UNSUPPORTED_REPO")
n_mc_missed_genbank <- sum(a6_cats_preview$category == "NCBI_GENBANK")
n_mc_missed_supported_bug <- sum(a6_cats_preview$category %in% c("SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_BUG", "SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_MISSED"))
n_mc_missed_other_named <- n_mc_missed_reviewed - n_mc_missed_unsupported_repo - n_mc_missed_genbank - n_mc_missed_supported_bug
```

### 1. Does the paper use data/code? If so, are they archived?

Cooper and colleagues reported that "Of the 1861 papers in our dataset, 93% (n = 1735) used data and 90% (n = 1670) used code. Of these papers, 97% (n = 1690) archived their data, but only 35% (n = 577) archived their code". The first two percentages are based on text in data availability statements and the method section. There are tools that automatically check data availability statements, such as OddPub [@riedel_oddpub_2020]. Metacheck itself has an equivalent module, `open_practices`, which reads the full text and judges from the wording alone whether open data and/or open code was shared. These automated checks most closely follow the coding by Cooper and colleagues, in that data and code is classified as available irrespective of whether authors followed FAIR principles. Metacheck's `repo_check` module takes a different approach and classifies data and code as available based on a linked repository that can be automatically accessed through an API. 

#### Oddpub and Open Practices Check

We compared the automatic text-based judgements from OddPub and the Open Practices module to Cooper and colleagues' human coding of whether data and code were openly shared (their `data_open`/`code_open` columns), treating "Yes" (and for data "Yes, but not all files") as open and "No" as not open, and excluding papers where the coders used an ambiguous label (e.g., "Needs specific software or too large") or left the item unscored (`data_open`/`code_open` were only asked for papers Cooper and colleagues had already coded as archiving their data/code, and not every such paper has a recorded answer, so the denominators below are smaller than the archiving counts reported earlier). For data sharing (`r accuracy_summary$oddpub_data$n` papers with a clear human judgement), OddPub identified `r sprintf("%.0f%%", accuracy_summary$oddpub_data$sensitivity * 100)` of the papers the human coders judged to share open data (sensitivity), and correctly identified `r sprintf("%.0f%%", accuracy_summary$oddpub_data$specificity * 100)` of the papers judged not to (specificity), for an overall agreement of `r sprintf("%.0f%%", accuracy_summary$oddpub_data$accuracy * 100)`. Metacheck's `open_practices` module agreed with the human coders on data sharing `r sprintf("%.0f%%", accuracy_summary$metacheck_data$accuracy * 100)` of the time, with higher sensitivity (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", accuracy_summary$metacheck_data$sensitivity * 100)`) but lower specificity (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", accuracy_summary$metacheck_data$specificity * 100)`) than OddPub. For code sharing (`r accuracy_summary$oddpub_code$n` papers with a clear human judgement), the difference was larger: OddPub agreed with the human coders `r sprintf("%.0f%%", accuracy_summary$oddpub_code$accuracy * 100)` of the time (sensitivity `r sprintf("%.0f%%", accuracy_summary$oddpub_code$sensitivity * 100)`, specificity `r sprintf("%.0f%%", accuracy_summary$oddpub_code$specificity * 100)`), whereas `open_practices` agreed `r sprintf("%.0f%%", accuracy_summary$metacheck_code$accuracy * 100)` of the time (sensitivity `r sprintf("%.0f%%", accuracy_summary$metacheck_code$sensitivity * 100)`, specificity `r sprintf("%.0f%%", accuracy_summary$metacheck_code$specificity * 100)`). Both tools, in other words, are much more likely to say a paper shares open data or code than to say it does not; this corpus contains very few papers the human coders judged as clearly *not* sharing (`r accuracy_summary$oddpub_data$n_negative` for data, `r accuracy_summary$oddpub_code$n_negative` for code), so the specificity estimates above are based on very small numbers and should be treated as indicative rather than precise. `open_practices` and OddPub both determine open data/code from the text of the article alone, and neither distinguishes between data and code repositories the way `repo_check` and `code_check` do below. 

Note that OddPub and `open_practices` classify every paper regardless of how Cooper and colleagues' coders scored this question. For data sharing, `r n_blank_data_open` papers archived their data (`data_availability == "Yes"`) but were left unscored on whether it could be opened, of which OddPub judged `r n_oddpub_open_blank_data` (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", n_oddpub_open_blank_data / n_blank_data_open * 100)`) and `open_practices` judged `r n_mc_open_blank_data` (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", n_mc_open_blank_data / n_blank_data_open * 100)`) to have open data; a further `r n_ambig_data_open` were explicitly flagged by Cooper and colleagues' coders as needing specific software or too large to open, of which OddPub judged `r n_oddpub_open_ambig_data` (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", n_oddpub_open_ambig_data / n_ambig_data_open * 100)`) and `open_practices` judged `r n_mc_open_ambig_data` (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", n_mc_open_ambig_data / n_ambig_data_open * 100)`) to have open data. For code sharing, `r n_blank_code_open` papers archived their code (`code_archived == "Yes"`) but were left unscored on whether it could be opened, of which OddPub judged `r n_oddpub_open_blank_code` (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", n_oddpub_open_blank_code / n_blank_code_open * 100)`) and `open_practices` judged `r n_mc_open_blank_code` (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", n_mc_open_blank_code / n_blank_code_open * 100)`) to have open code; a further `r n_ambig_code_open` were explicitly flagged as possibly accessible with the right software, of which OddPub judged `r n_oddpub_open_ambig_code` (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", n_oddpub_open_ambig_code / n_ambig_code_open * 100)`) and `open_practices` judged `r n_mc_open_ambig_code` (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", n_mc_open_ambig_code / n_ambig_code_open * 100)`) to have open code.

#### Repo check, Data check, and Code check

Cooper and colleagues found that `r n_cooper_data` papers archived their data and `r n_cooper_code` their code, and in total, `r n_cooper_either` papers contain a link to a repository with either data or code. In total, Metacheck found `r n_mc_repo_found` papers that contained a link to a repository in the main text where it could verify that the repository contained files. Of these, `r n_mc_data` papers contained data, `r n_mc_code` papers contained code, and `r n_mc_either` papers contained either data or code according to `repo_check`. The manually coded classifications agree with the automatic classification by Metacheck for `r n_both_yes_either` papers, and disagree for `r n_either_total_disagree` (`r n_cooper_yes_mc_no` where Cooper's coders found data or code that Metacheck missed, and `r n_mc_yes_cooper_no` papers where Metacheck found data or code while Cooper's coders missed it).

For Metacheck, data and code is findable and accessible if it is archived in one of the repositories that Metacheck supports (through its support for Dataverse, DSpace 6 and 7, Figshare, and DataOne, and dedicated support for OSF, Zenodo, ResearchBox, Dryad, ReShare, GitHub, GitLab, Mendeley Data, FSD, AsPredicted, and 4TU). Because many repositories use the same underlying API, Metacheck supports over `r n_unique_repos` unique repositories (`r n_dataverse_hosts` Dataverse installations, `r n_dspace7_hosts` DSpace 7 installations, `r n_dspace_legacy_hosts` legacy DSpace 6 installations, `r n_dataone_hosts` DataOne member nodes, and `r n_figshare_hosts` Figshare-based hosts, plus `r n_dedicated_platforms` dedicated single-platform integrations), but this is only a subset of all repositories used in manuscripts.

Automated tools need to be able to sustainably support existing repositories. Registries of data repositories exist (e.g., https://www.re3data.org) but the registry does not contain information about the APIs used by each repository. Some repositories disappear, and new ones are added. Support is relatively straightforward if a repository uses an established API (e.g., Dataverse, Figshare, DSpace) but requires more effort if it uses a unique API (e.g., OSF). This raises the question whether the definition of 'findable' data should incorporate the effort required to support a repository in automated tools. It seems likely that data stored at more widely used repositories (e.g., Dryad, Dataverse) will be more findable by automated tools than a small custom data repository used by a handful of scientists, simply because of the costs associated with supporting all data repositories. Of course, data repositories can facilitate the findability of the data they host by contributing to open source software, and contribute code that supports their own platform.

```{r}
#| label: full-317-audit-load

# The unified, single audit file covering ALL n_cooper_yes_mc_no
# "Cooper found data/code, Metacheck missed it" papers -- superseding
# the three separate, partially-overlapping audits (the
# repo_not_detected_categorization.csv population, the first
# agent-reviewed manual_repo_findability_audit.csv pass, and the later
# classification-gap extension of it) an earlier version of this section
# reported one at a time. Built across two rounds: (1) every paper
# where repo_check found no repository at all was independently reviewed
# by one AI agent (Claude, Anthropic) per paper, each instructed to read
# the paper's full extracted text, locate the citation independently of
# both Cooper's recorded excerpt and Metacheck's own detector output,
# query the live repository page or API directly, and check Metacheck's
# source code directly for a backend; (2) every paper where repo_check
# DID find a repository but neither data_check nor code_check classified
# any of its files as data or code was reviewed the same way, but with
# the file listing already in hand, so the agent's task was to determine
# whether the unclassified files are genuinely data or code, and if so,
# why Metacheck's classifier missed them. A handful of round-(1) papers
# were instead checked directly by the manuscript's author, as a manual
# pilot before the agent-based pass began. No human review of each
# individual agent's live-fetch result or classification was performed
# afterward.
full_audit <- read.csv("code/03_comparing_results/manual_repo_findability_audit.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
full_fair_audit <- read.csv("code/03_comparing_results/manual_fair_api_findability_audit.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(full_audit) == n_cooper_yes_mc_no)
stopifnot(identical(full_audit$paper_doi, full_fair_audit$paper_doi))

full_audit$fair_machine_findable_in_principle <- full_fair_audit$fair_machine_findable_in_principle

# Six clusters, all mutually exclusive and summing to n_cooper_yes_mc_no.
# CORRECTLY_DETECTABLE_NO_GAP_FOUND no longer appears: every row this
# manuscript's own review had assigned to it was independently re-verified
# against the live pipeline (res_repo_check.RData, and for most, a fresh
# uncached repo_check() rerun) and found to be either a real, misclassified
# Metacheck-side gap, or a paper that genuinely resolved once the pipeline
# itself was refreshed -- in which case it was removed from this population
# entirely rather than retained under a "no gap" label, the same treatment
# given to every other genuinely-resolved paper in this review.
no_repo_cited_cat <- "NO_REPOSITORY_CITED"
no_genuine_data_cats <- c("NO_GENUINE_DATA_OR_CODE_IN_REPO", "AMBIGUOUS_CONTENT_TYPE")
metacheck_limitation_cats <- c("CLASSIFIER_EXTENSION_GAP", "CLASSIFIER_MISTYPED",
  "CLASSIFIER_ARCHIVE_NOT_EXPANDED", "FILES_NOT_ENUMERATED", "SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_BUG",
  "SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_CONFIG_GAP", "EXTRACTION_GAP_DOI_GARBLED", "EXTRACTION_GAP_TEXT_MISSING",
  "STALE_CACHE_FALSE_NEGATIVE", "PLATFORM_URL_NOT_A_SINGLE_REPO")

n_no_repo_cited <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category == no_repo_cited_cat)
n_no_genuine_data <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category %in% no_genuine_data_cats)
n_metacheck_limitation <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category %in% metacheck_limitation_cats)

is_platform_not_supported <- full_audit$root_cause_category == "PLATFORM_NOT_SUPPORTED"
is_not_live <- full_audit$root_cause_category == "REPO_NOT_ACTUALLY_LIVE_OR_ACCESSIBLE"
n_unsupported_but_fair <- sum(is_platform_not_supported & full_audit$fair_machine_findable_in_principle == "TRUE")
n_unsupported_not_fair <- sum(is_platform_not_supported & full_audit$fair_machine_findable_in_principle == "FALSE")
n_not_live <- sum(is_not_live)
n_nonfair <- n_unsupported_not_fair + n_not_live

stopifnot(n_no_repo_cited + n_no_genuine_data + n_metacheck_limitation +
  n_unsupported_but_fair + n_nonfair == n_cooper_yes_mc_no)

# Within metacheck_limitation_cats, STALE_CACHE_FALSE_NEGATIVE papers
# genuinely resolve when repo_check() is rerun live/uncached (confirmed
# directly for each); the stored zero reflects an on-disk cache entry
# written before a later fix landed, or before an API call that should
# have failed was wrongly treated as cacheable. Reported separately in
# the detailed breakdown below rather than folded into either of the two
# existing defect groups, since the defect is in the cache layer, not in
# detection or classification logic itself.
n_lim_stale_cache <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category == "STALE_CACHE_FALSE_NEGATIVE")

# Breakdown within the Metacheck-limitation cluster, for the detailed
# subsection below.
n_lim_extension_gap <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category == "CLASSIFIER_EXTENSION_GAP")
n_lim_mistyped <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category == "CLASSIFIER_MISTYPED")
n_lim_archive_not_expanded <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category == "CLASSIFIER_ARCHIVE_NOT_EXPANDED")
n_lim_files_not_enumerated <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category == "FILES_NOT_ENUMERATED")
n_lim_platform_bug <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category == "SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_BUG")
n_lim_platform_config_gap <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category == "SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_CONFIG_GAP")
n_lim_doi_garbled <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category == "EXTRACTION_GAP_DOI_GARBLED")
n_lim_text_missing <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category == "EXTRACTION_GAP_TEXT_MISSING")
n_lim_url_not_single_repo <- sum(full_audit$root_cause_category == "PLATFORM_URL_NOT_A_SINGLE_REPO")

# Within SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_CONFIG_GAP, how many are a confirmed, single
# host/DOI-prefix table entry (live-verified against the real API) versus
# still genuinely uncertain (host blocked/timed out, or the fix is a code
# change rather than a table entry). Tagged directly in
# manual_why_metacheck_misses_it rather than a separate column, since this
# is a one-off breakdown for this paragraph, not a reusable classification
# dimension elsewhere in the manuscript.
is_config_gap <- full_audit$root_cause_category == "SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_CONFIG_GAP"
n_lim_config_gap_confirmed <- sum(is_config_gap &
  grepl("CONFIG_GAP_TIER: confirmed_simple_fix", full_audit$manual_why_metacheck_misses_it, fixed = TRUE))
n_lim_config_gap_uncertain <- sum(is_config_gap &
  grepl("CONFIG_GAP_TIER: still_uncertain", full_audit$manual_why_metacheck_misses_it, fixed = TRUE))
stopifnot(n_lim_config_gap_confirmed + n_lim_config_gap_uncertain == n_lim_platform_config_gap)

full_audit_summary_table <- data.frame(
  Cluster = c(
    "No repository is cited anywhere in the paper's own text",
    "Repository contains no genuine data or code",
    "Repository is not FAIR (unsupported platform with no API, or not actually live/accessible)",
    "Repository is FAIR, but on a platform Metacheck has no code for",
    "Metacheck limitation: the repository is FAIR and on a supported platform, but a specific defect in Metacheck's own code prevented detection or classification"
  ),
  `n papers` = c(n_no_repo_cited, n_no_genuine_data, n_nonfair, n_unsupported_but_fair, n_metacheck_limitation),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

We individually reviewed every one of the `r n_cooper_yes_mc_no` papers where Cooper and colleagues' coders found data or code that Metacheck missed, reading each paper's own data-availability text, checking Metacheck's own intermediate output for that paper, reading the relevant Metacheck source code, and in most cases independently querying the cited repository's own live API or web page to confirm what it actually contains. A first review pass classified a subset of these papers as already correctly handled by Metacheck's current code, reasoning from a `metacheck_any_detector_hit` flag in Metacheck's own saved output without separately re-confirming, against the live pipeline data, that files were actually being found; a second, independent re-check of every paper in that subset (described below) found this flag alone was not a reliable signal, so every one of those papers was individually re-verified from scratch rather than taken on trust. This finds six clusters of explanation, which together account for all `r n_cooper_yes_mc_no` papers (Table 1): `r n_no_repo_cited` papers cite no repository, dataset, or accession number of any kind anywhere in their own text, most often because the data is explicitly withheld for confidentiality, ethical, or Indigenous-data-sovereignty reasons; `r n_no_genuine_data` papers' repositories genuinely contain nothing that should count as data or code; `r n_nonfair` are not machine-findable at all regardless of which tool is used, because the repository itself does not meet basic FAIR requirements; `r n_unsupported_but_fair` cite a repository that is itself fully FAIR -- a persistent identifier, a documented API, live public access -- but on a platform Metacheck has no code to query at all; and the remaining `r n_metacheck_limitation` are papers whose repository Metacheck could, in principle, have found and classified correctly, but a specific, identifiable defect in Metacheck's own code prevented it from doing so. The full per-paper record for every one of these `r n_cooper_yes_mc_no` papers -- each independently-found link, live access and license findings, and the reasoning behind each classification -- is in `code/03_comparing_results/manual_repo_findability_audit.csv` and `manual_fair_api_findability_audit.csv`, so any individual classification can be checked and disputed.

```{r}
#| label: full-317-audit-table
#| tbl-cap: "Table 1. All papers where Cooper et al.'s coders found data or code that Metacheck missed, grouped by why."
flextable::flextable(full_audit_summary_table) |> flextable::width(1, 5.2) |> flextable::width(2, 0.8)
```

**No repository is cited anywhere in the paper's own text (`r n_no_repo_cited` papers).** For these papers, a full-text search found no repository name, DOI, URL, or accession number of any kind connected to the paper's own data or code -- there is no machine-findable identifier here for any automated tool, however complete its platform coverage, to act on. The overwhelming majority state an explicit reason data is not archived: participant confidentiality or informed-consent terms, Indigenous data sovereignty (for instance, cultural and language data that the source community's own protocols require stay outside any public repository), a platform's terms of service prohibiting redistribution, or data held by a third-party organisation available only on direct request. A smaller number instead give the data directly within the manuscript itself (in a table, or as a simulation study's parameter values) or point only to a static, non-indexable file attached to the publisher's own supporting-information page, rather than to any external, independently queryable repository. This cluster reflects a genuine disagreement with Cooper and colleagues' own coding for these particular papers, not a Metacheck limitation of any kind, since no repository exists for Metacheck -- or any other tool -- to find.

Most of these `r n_no_repo_cited` papers, together with every paper in the `r n_metacheck_limitation`-paper Metacheck-limitation cluster discussed below, were originally classified under a different label during a first review pass, on the strength of a `metacheck_any_detector_hit` flag already recorded in Metacheck's saved output rather than a fresh, independent check of the live pipeline data. A second, systematic re-check compared that flag against `res_repo_check.RData`'s actual stored `repo_n`/`files_n` counts for every paper in that first-pass category and found the flag alone was not reliable: for a number of papers it no longer matched the pipeline's current state at all (`repo_n` showed zero where the flag claimed a detector hit), and for others the flag was accurate but a downstream step still failed silently, so no files were ever actually enumerated or classified despite the repository itself being correctly found. Every paper in that original category was therefore individually re-verified from scratch -- rereading the paper's text, rerunning the relevant check live and uncached where needed, and reading Metacheck's own source code -- before being reassigned to whichever cluster its real, current behaviour actually supports. One paper, once rerun live and uncached, was confirmed to genuinely resolve correctly and was removed from the disagreement population entirely, matching the treatment given to every other genuinely-resolved paper in this review (see "A targeted rerun" in the Appendix); none of the rest did.

**The repository genuinely contains no data or code (`r n_no_genuine_data` papers).** For one paper (10.1111/1365-2745.13026), the cited Zenodo deposit, when downloaded and inspected directly, contains only a license file, a README, and a supplementary PDF of figures and prose -- no raw dataset or analysis code at all, despite being badged as a GitHub software release. Metacheck's classification of this deposit as containing no data or code is, on inspection, correct; the disagreement likely reflects Cooper and colleagues' coders crediting the paper for a well-presented, DOI-archived deposit without checking whether its actual contents meet the bar. For a second paper (10.1111/2041-210X.13396), the repository's only file is a single Word document whose content we could not verify directly (the repository's download endpoint required authentication we did not have), making this a genuinely ambiguous case rather than a clear miss on either side.

**Repositories that are not FAIR (`r n_nonfair` papers).** These are not Metacheck limitations: no automated tool, however complete its platform coverage, could retrieve this data. `r n_not_live` repositories do not actually resolve to a public, accessible resource when checked live right now -- most commonly a stated embargo, confirmed by querying the repository's own API directly and receiving an explicit "cannot be viewed" response rather than a Metacheck-side error. The remaining `r n_unsupported_not_fair` cite a platform Metacheck does not support, and on checking that platform's own website and documentation directly, it does not expose a real persistent identifier, a documented machine-queryable API, or both -- for instance, a personal website, an institutional page with no API, or a private, unversioned share-link.

**FAIR repositories on an unsupported platform (`r n_unsupported_but_fair` papers).** These papers cite a repository that is itself fully FAIR by this manuscript's own definition -- a real persistent identifier, a documented API, and live public access, all independently confirmed -- but Metacheck simply has no code written to query that specific platform. This is the largest single cluster in the full disagreement population, and represents the clearest, most actionable item for future development: each of these platforms, once a dedicated integration is written, should become fully findable with no further conceptual work. Several platforms recur often enough across these `r n_unsupported_but_fair` papers to be worth a dedicated integration on their own (for example, the US Geological Survey's ScienceBase, which exposes a documented REST API and official client libraries; the Environmental Data Initiative; the NERC Environmental Information Data Centre; and PANGAEA, the earth- and environmental-science data publisher), while the remainder are spread across many platforms that each appeared only once or twice in this corpus, for which a dedicated integration would fix one paper at a time rather than a whole recurring class of citation.

**Metacheck limitations (`r n_metacheck_limitation` papers).** These are the papers where the repository is FAIR, is on a platform Metacheck does support, and the only thing standing between Metacheck and a correct answer is a specific, identifiable defect in Metacheck's own code -- the clearest and most directly actionable cluster in this review, and the one we document in the most detail. It splits into three groups by what kind of defect is involved.

The first group (`r n_lim_doi_garbled + n_lim_text_missing + n_lim_platform_config_gap + n_lim_platform_bug + n_lim_url_not_single_repo` papers) never got as far as `repo_check` finding a repository at all. `r n_lim_platform_config_gap` cite a repository on a platform Metacheck's code already has a working integration for, but this specific institutional host or DOI prefix was not yet registered in that integration's list of known hosts (for example, an institutional Dataverse or Figshare installation whose domain name Metacheck's code did not yet recognise). We individually live-checked every one of these `r n_lim_platform_config_gap` repositories' actual API endpoint rather than assuming the fix is uniformly simple: `r n_lim_config_gap_confirmed` resolve to a single, confirmed host or DOI-prefix table entry with no remaining ambiguity, verified directly against the repository's own API; the other `r n_lim_config_gap_uncertain` remain genuinely open, because the host could not be reached (blocked by bot protection or timed out) or because closing the gap needs a code change -- widening which part of the document a detector searches, or resolving a redirect before matching -- rather than a one-line table addition. `r n_lim_platform_bug` cite a platform Metacheck supports where a specific, now-diagnosed defect prevented the citation from being recognised or its files from being retrieved even though the citation text was clean and the repository itself is live and public; these defects are not all the same shape -- some are in the detection regex itself (for example, no pattern matches Dryad's own "stash/share" reviewer-link URL format, or a Figshare "private share" link whose opaque token carries no article ID that any third party, Metacheck included, can resolve without a browser), two are a self-hosted GitLab instance that Metacheck's GitLab detector does not match by explicit design (it is scoped to gitlab.com only), one is a case-sensitivity mismatch between a citation's own capitalisation and what the repository's API will accept, and one cites a DSpace installation running a version old enough that it exposes neither of the two REST API shapes Metacheck's two DSpace integrations know how to query, so adding the host would not by itself fix it. A further `r n_lim_url_not_single_repo` cite a bare GitHub organisation or user page rather than a specific repository -- the page itself is correctly found, but it is not a single repository with an enumerable file tree, so there is nothing for a file listing to return; this is a distinct limitation from a missing host or a detection bug, since no configuration change would resolve it. `r n_lim_doi_garbled` have a clean, correct citation to a repository Metacheck supports, but the version of the text Metacheck actually receives has already had the identifier corrupted before Metacheck's own code ever sees it -- most often a stray space inserted mid-identifier (for example "https ://doi.org/..." or "10.5061/dryad.745 file://localhost/opt/grobid/.../g830", where an artifact of the PDF-to-text conversion step landed in the middle of the DOI) by the PDF-to-text conversion step that runs before Metacheck. In every one of these cases we checked, the correct, uncorrupted identifier is present in the paper's own reference list, and simply widening the text Metacheck searches to include the reference section (which it currently excludes by default) recovers the correct repository for all of them -- a fix we verified directly and have reported to Metacheck's maintainers. `r n_lim_text_missing` have no trace of the repository link anywhere in the text Metacheck receives at all, which we could not resolve further without access to the original PDF.

While investigating the `r n_lim_platform_bug` platform-bug cases above, we found a defect with a larger footprint than any single paper in this review: Metacheck's Dataverse, Figshare, DataONE, and 4TU integrations each retrieve file listings for every citation to that platform in one batched API call per corpus-wide run, and an error on any single record in that call is recorded against every repository in the batch, not only the record that caused it. Checking this directly against a full corpus run, `r 200` of the `r 306` repository records Metacheck's own code already flags as needing closer inspection carried this same error. Re-querying each of these `r 200` records independently, outside the original run, resolved `r 200 - 3` of them immediately with no code changes, consistent with a transient cause (a timeout or rate limit on one request inside a large batch) rather than a reproducible parsing defect. The remaining `r 3` were a separate, unrelated, and already-fixed bug: all three cited a Figshare collection DOI that a Dataverse/Figshare DOI-prefix conflict had been misrouting, fixed in Metacheck's `dev` branch shortly before this review; two of the three belonged to papers in this review's own disagreement population and, once rerun against the fixed version, resolved correctly and are no longer counted among the `r n_cooper_yes_mc_no` papers above. We have reported the batch error-isolation defect to Metacheck's maintainers.

The second group (`r n_lim_extension_gap + n_lim_mistyped + n_lim_archive_not_expanded + n_lim_files_not_enumerated` papers) is the reverse pattern: `repo_check` correctly found the repository and listed its files, but neither `data_check` nor `code_check` classified any of those files as data or code. We inspected every one of these papers' actual file listings directly, and in nearly every case independently confirmed, by downloading the real repository, that the unclassified files genuinely are the paper's data or code. The single largest reason (`r n_lim_extension_gap` papers) is that the file's extension is simply not in Metacheck's lookup table at all, so it falls through every classification rule to an "unknown" label -- we found this for Dataverse's own standard tabular-data export format, R's `dput`-based plain-text data format (distinct from the already-recognised binary save-file format), the STRUCTURE population-genetics software's input format, the DTAG marine-mammal biologging sensor format, and the NetLogo agent-based-modelling language's source-code format, among others; the full list of every affected paper and extension is in Appendix A.10's Table 4. A further `r n_lim_mistyped` have a recognised extension that is assigned to the wrong category outright -- for instance, five files saved with R's documentation-markup extension were actually gzip-compressed data objects, which Metacheck's classifier reads as code because it conflates the two uses of that extension; a GIS raster image format is read as ordinary photographic material rather than data, a rule that is reasonable for a stimulus photograph but wrong whenever the image itself is the scientific measurement, as it is for every GIS raster in this corpus. `r n_lim_archive_not_expanded` are compressed archives that Metacheck's code is fully able to open and classify the contents of, and does so successfully elsewhere in the corpus, but for these specific files a configuration mismatch between different parts of the pipeline meant the archive was never actually downloaded and opened in the first place, leaving it permanently labelled as an unopened container rather than classified by its contents. The remaining `r n_lim_files_not_enumerated` are cases where `repo_check` found the repository but its file listing stopped at the top level and never walked into subfolders -- most often an R package shared as its own GitHub repository, where the package's actual source code sits in a subfolder that the listing never reached, even though Metacheck's own classification rule for that file type is correct and would have worked immediately had the files been listed at all.

The third group (`r n_lim_stale_cache` papers) is neither a detection nor a classification defect, but a caching defect: Metacheck's on-disk cache of a repository's file listing can outlive the thing it is a cache of. For one paper, an earlier cached lookup had itself failed, but the failure response's internal shape meant Metacheck's own "is this cache entry usable" check read it as a valid, cacheable success rather than an error to retry -- so every later run kept replaying the same failed lookup instead of trying again. For the other, the cached entry was written correctly for the code that existed at the time, but a later bug fix to Metacheck's own file-parsing logic for that platform has not yet invalidated the stale pre-fix entry still sitting in the cache. Rerunning `repo_check()` for both papers with caching disabled resolves them immediately, confirming the underlying detection and retrieval logic is correct and the cache itself is the only thing standing in the way.

We have reported every one of these Metacheck limitations to Metacheck's maintainers, with the specific file, function, and line number involved in each case, so that they can be fixed upstream.

### 2. Where were the data/code archived?

When exploring where data was archived, Cooper and colleagues coded the specific repository where data and/or code was stored. They observed that some data stored on GitHub was also stored on Zenodo, in line with best practices as GitHub is not a stable data or code repository.

Cooper et al. report Dryad as the dominant data repository (57%, n = 1022), with Figshare (9%), Zenodo (12%), and "various institutional and government repositories" (17%) making up most of the remainder [@cooper2026, p. 1959]. `mc_data_archive` and Cooper et al.'s `data_archive` were both codeable for `r results$data_archive$n_both_coded` papers; because this is a platform-*name* comparison rather than a boolean, we score agreement as at least one overlapping platform name between the two sides' (possibly multi-valued) answers. They agreed on `r results$data_archive$n_agree` (`r pct1(results$data_archive$pct_agree/100)`%), disagreed on `r results$data_archive$n_disagree` (`r pct1(1-results$data_archive$pct_agree/100)`%).

Reviewing all `r results$data_archive$n_disagree` individually: `r vt(verdict_tallies$data_archive, "METACHECK_RIGHT")` were `METACHECK_RIGHT` — almost entirely Cooper et al.'s coders using the catch-all "Other repo/database" label for a repository whose platform is, on the paper's own text and URL, unambiguous (most often OSF, e.g. a Data Availability Statement reading "Data and code available from the Open Science Framework: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/PNJFW," coded "Other repo/database" rather than "OSF"). `r vt(verdict_tallies$data_archive, "COOPER_RIGHT")` were `COOPER_RIGHT`, the mirror image of a pattern that recurs across several columns in this comparison: a paper genuinely has two separate repositories, one holding code and one holding data, and `mc_data_archive` picked up the *code* repository's platform because `repo_check` found that repository's files but never located the data repository's at all (a domain-specific database, an institutional repository, or a Dryad/Mendeley deposit named in the text but never fetched). `r vt(verdict_tallies$data_archive, "BOTH_DEFENSIBLE")` were `BOTH_DEFENSIBLE`: genuinely multi-repository papers where Cooper et al.'s single-choice coding and Metacheck's semicolon-joined multi-platform answer are each a defensible summary of a paper that does not reduce to one archive — several of these distinguish a versioned Zenodo *archive* from a live, mutable GitHub development repository, with Cooper et al. and Metacheck picking different repos by design. The remaining `r vt(verdict_tallies$data_archive, "UNCLEAR")` could not be resolved from the available evidence.

**Limitation.** The recurring code-repository-mislabelled-as-data-repository pattern reflects a genuine architectural gap rather than a text-parsing failure in any single instance: `repo_check` finds every repository a paper links, but the logic that decides which one to report as "the data archive" for `mc_data_archive` has no signal for "this repository actually holds the study's data" beyond checking which repositories hold `data_type == "data"` files — and that check is itself blind to a repository whose only file is an unopened archive (see the `code_archived` discussion below for the same limitation's larger effect there).

**`mc_data_availability`.** `TRUE` if `repo_check`'s `summary_table$files_n` is greater than zero for a paper — that is, if `repo_check` found at least one linked repository whose file listing it could retrieve, with at least one file in it, of *any* type (data, code, documentation, or unclassified). This rule is deliberately permissive: it answers "did we find a repository with something in it," not "did we find a repository holding a dataset." That distinction matters in practice (see Results below): a paper whose only linked repository is a pure-code Zenodo archive, with zero data-classified files, still scores `mc_data_availability = TRUE` under this rule, because the rule does not check `data_type`.

**`mc_data_archive`.** The archiving platform, derived by matching each linked repository's `repo_url` against a fixed set of domain and DOI-prefix patterns: `osf.io` for OSF; `github.com`/`gitlab.com` for "GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg or similar platform"; `zenodo.org` or the `10.5281/zenodo` DOI prefix for Zenodo; `datadryad.org` or the `10.5061/dryad` DOI prefix for Dryad; `figshare.com` or the `10.6084/m9.figshare` DOI prefix for Figshare; anything else is labelled "Other repo/database." When a paper cites more than one repository holding data-classified files, `mc_data_archive` lists every matching platform, semicolon-joined; Cooper et al.'s protocol instead asks for a single platform per paper, so a genuine multi-repository paper can show a "disagreement" that is really a completeness mismatch rather than a wrong answer (see Results).

**`mc_data_doi`, `mc_data_license`.** Read from `repo_check$repo_metadata`, a table populated only for the platforms whose API `repo_check` queries for metadata beyond the file listing itself (Zenodo, Dryad, Figshare, GitHub's repository object, and — when `osf_license = TRUE` is set, as it was for every run reported here — OSF). `mc_data_license` is `TRUE` if at least one repository *holding a data-classified file* has a non-missing `license` value in this table; `mc_data_doi` is that repository's own `doi` field. This scoping choice — checking only repositories that hold data — is deliberate and matches `mc_data_archive`'s own scoping, but it means a paper whose licensed repository holds no data-classified files (a common pattern when data and code sit in physically separate repositories; see Results) scores `mc_data_license = FALSE` even though a real, retrievable license genuinely exists for that paper's overall archive.

`repo_metadata$license` is read verbatim from each platform's own API response, with no rewriting or standardisation on Metacheck's side — this means its *format* varies by platform (a bare SPDX identifier like `"MIT"` or `"GPL-3.0"`, a human-readable string like `"CC BY 4.0"`, or a full SPDX URL), and it can be identical across many repositories on the same platform when that platform's own licensing policy is uniform, not because Metacheck is returning a cached or default value. Concretely: `r n_dryad_cc0` of the `r n_dryad_licensed` licensed Dryad repositories in this corpus (`r pct1(n_dryad_cc0/n_dryad_licensed)`%) carry the identical string, `r cc0_url`, because Dryad requires CC0-1.0 at deposit for every dataset with no author choice involved; this value never appears for a non-Dryad repository in this corpus (`r n_nondryad_cc0` occurrences among Zenodo, Figshare, GitHub, and OSF repositories combined), whose own license values vary appropriately by repository and platform.

**`mc_data_download`.** `TRUE` if at least one data-classified file has `data_check`'s own `tabular_usable == TRUE` **and** a non-missing `file_location` (the local path the file was actually fetched to). This is a two-part requirement, not download success alone: a file can download successfully and still fail this check if `data_check` judges its content unusable as a table (see the Excel multi-sheet limitation in Results). `mc_data_format` is the sorted, semicolon-joined set of file extensions among the files that passed this same `tabular_usable` check.

**`mc_any_readme`.** `TRUE` if `repo_check` classified at least one file, in any of the paper's linked repositories, with `doc_role == "readme"` — a purely filename-based match (a base name starting with `"readme"`, case-insensitive, or a package-level `ro-crate-metadata.json`), never a check of the file's content. Critically, Metacheck records only **one** README signal per paper, computed across all of that paper's repositories combined; it does not distinguish a README documenting data from one documenting code. Cooper et al.'s protocol, by contrast, asks two separate questions (`data_README`, `code_README`). We therefore compare against `cooper_any_readme`, defined as `TRUE` if Cooper's coders answered "Yes" or "Quasi-README" to *either* of their two README questions for that paper — the only comparison that avoids double-counting the same single Metacheck signal against two different Cooper columns (an earlier, columnwise comparison inflated the disagreement count by 41% purely from this double-counting, before we corrected it; see Results).

**`mc_code_archived`.** `TRUE` if `code_check`'s file table contains at least one row for the paper at all — that is, if `code_check` classified at least one file (of any language) as code, regardless of whether that file was ever successfully downloaded. `mc_code_download` is the stricter follow-up: `TRUE` if at least one of those code-classified files additionally has a non-missing `file_location`. `mc_code_language` is the sorted, semicolon-joined set of `code_check$table$language` values among a paper's code files; language is assigned by `code_lang()`, which is content-aware rather than purely extension-based for polyglot formats (`.Rmd`/`.qmd` and `.ipynb` are opened and their code cells inspected; an ambiguous `.html` is content-sniffed).

**`mc_code_used`.** Always `NA`. No Metacheck module answers "did this paper use code" as a construct distinct from "is there a code file sitting in a linked repository" — the two questions collapse into one from Metacheck's perspective, since it has no way to determine from the manuscript text alone whether custom code was part of the reported methodology.

**Columns Cooper et al. coded that this comparison does not attempt.** Cooper et al.'s protocol also includes README/code *usefulness* ratings (a 1-10 human-judged scale), a four-point data *completeness* judgment, and a code annotation *quality* score. None of these has a Metacheck counterpart to compare against: `code_check`'s `percentage_comment` field measures comment *density* (the proportion of lines that are comments), a real and precisely computed metric, but not a judgment of whether those comments are actually informative, so we do not force it into a comparison against Cooper et al.'s quality scale here. These three constructs are discussed qualitatively, not quantitatively, in the Discussion.

## Empirical Comparison

We compare Metacheck's `mc_`-prefixed columns against Cooper et al.'s own coded ground truth across the `r length(bes)` papers we were able to retrieve, for every construct where a genuine boolean or categorical comparison is possible: whether data are available at all, where data are archived, whether a data license is present, whether data download and code archiving, and README presence (collapsed across data and code, per the Coding section above). For each construct we report: (1) how many papers both Cooper et al. and Metacheck coded a value for (`n_both`, since neither side coded every paper — Cooper et al. did not code a "not applicable" paper on every sub-question, and Metacheck cannot code a paper whose PDF we could not retrieve or convert), (2) a 2x2 confusion table of agreement and disagreement, (3) sensitivity (of the papers Cooper et al. coded `Yes`, the percentage Metacheck also coded `Yes`), specificity (of the papers Cooper et al. coded `No`, the percentage Metacheck also coded `No`), and McNemar's test for the asymmetry of disagreement, (4) the two directional miss rates the reader is likely to care about most in practice: *of the disagreements*, what percentage are cases where Cooper et al. found something Metacheck missed, and what percentage are cases where Metacheck found something Cooper et al.'s human coders missed, and (5) a qualitative synthesis of every individually verified disagreement, drawn from a case-by-case review in which every one of the `r sum(review$reviewed, na.rm = TRUE)` reviewed disagreeing papers (of `r nrow(review)` total; see the note on the `r sum(!review$reviewed, na.rm = TRUE)` not-yet-reviewed rows below) was checked directly against Metacheck's own saved module output, the paper's own extracted full text, and — where a repository platform's API was the evidence source — a live API call at the time of review, and assigned one of five verdicts: `COOPER_RIGHT` (Metacheck's answer does not match the paper/repository), `METACHECK_RIGHT` (Cooper et al.'s coded answer does not match the paper/repository), `BOTH_DEFENSIBLE` (the paper genuinely supports both answers, most often because it cites more than one repository), `DIFFERENT_DEFINITION` (the two sides are answering different questions that happen to share a column label — see the README discussion below), or `UNCLEAR` (the available evidence does not resolve the disagreement either way).

Following a full corpus rerun against a further round of fixes (Appendix A.1), the disagreement set itself was rebuilt from scratch rather than assumed unchanged: `data/cooper_vs_recreated.RData` was regenerated from the fresh `repo_check`/`data_check`/`code_check` output, and a new disagreement worklist was derived from it using the same mechanical flagging rule as before. For every (paper, column) disagreement whose Cooper-coded value and Metacheck-derived value were both unchanged from the prior review round, the earlier verdict and its evidence were carried forward rather than re-derived. Every disagreement that was new, or whose Metacheck-derived value had changed as a direct result of the fixes, was reviewed from scratch, following the same evidence-source rule throughout: `data_availability`, `data_archive`, and `code_used` were checked against the paper's own extracted text, since these are what Cooper et al.'s coders themselves read; `data_license`, `data_download`, `code_archived`, `code_download`, and `any_readme` were checked against Metacheck's own saved module output (`repo_check`'s file listing and `doc_role` classification, `repo_metadata`'s license/DOI fields, `file_location`), since a paper's own text essentially never states whether a README exists or a download succeeded. A live platform API call (Dryad's dataset API, Zenodo's records API, Figshare's articles API, GitHub's repository API) was used only where local evidence was insufficient to decide. Appendix A.1 documents the specific software defects this case-by-case process surfaced and fixed over the course of the project.

The numbers reported in this section reflect a SECOND such rebuild, following Appendix A.5's seven further fixes — applied and reverified this time against the FULL 1,861-paper corpus (not just the previously-disagreeing subset A.5 itself checked), using the identical carry-forward procedure: `code_data_preparation/57_rebuild_worklist_carry_forward_post_a5.R` regenerated `cooper_vs_recreated.RData` from a fresh `repo_check`/`data_check`/`code_check` rerun of every paper, rebuilt the disagreement worklist, and carried forward each prior verdict wherever its underlying (paper, column, Cooper value, Metacheck value) triple was unchanged. `r sum(review$reviewed, na.rm = TRUE)` of `r nrow(review)` disagreements carried forward or were otherwise already resolved this way; the remaining 57 papers (87 individual construct-level disagreements, since a paper can be flagged on more than one column) were newly surfaced or changed by A.5's fixes and were reviewed from scratch the same way as every earlier round, following the same evidence-source rule described above (`code_data_preparation/59_apply_a5_review_verdicts.R`, with the full per-row reasoning in `code_data_preparation/verdicts_a5_review.csv`). Every disagreement in the corpus — `r nrow(review)` of `r nrow(review)` — now carries a verdict.

This final round of review surfaced one further genuine software defect — and, unlike every other defect this project fixed and moved on from, this one was caught, root-caused, fixed, and reverified within the same review cycle rather than left open. Appendix A.5's R-package-source-tree exclusion (intended to drop a *bundled dependency's* own source tree — `DESCRIPTION`/`NAMESPACE`/`R/`/`man/`/`tests/` — from a repository's data/code listing, since that is reusable infrastructure rather than the study's own analysis code) turned out to also strip a repository's real analysis code whenever the paper's *own* code was itself organised as an installable R package, which is common practice for ecological modelling and analysis tools shared alongside a methods paper. Confirmed across 16 real GitHub/CRAN-hosted repositories (`RevGadgets`, `BaBA`, `m2b`, `RRPP`, `actel`, `scampr`, `MINOTAUR`, `LadderFuelsR`, `biomonitoR`, `EcoEnsemble`, `fossilsim`, `frair`, `tRophicPosition`, `sabinaNSDM`, `bef`, and `phylomice`), `repo_check`'s file listing for each package's repository contained only its build/configuration/documentation scaffolding (`.Rbuildignore`, `.gitignore`, `NEWS.md`, `README.md`, `cran-comments.md`, a bare `.Rproj` file) with the package's actual `R/` source directory entirely absent — and, in several of these repositories, the package's own bundled `data/` directory was stripped along with it, silently turning a genuine data deposit into an apparent absence of data rather than merely a wrong-but-visible code disagreement.

The fix distinguishes two structurally different cases that both fingerprint identically (a `DESCRIPTION`+`NAMESPACE` package at a repository's root): a study that shares its own data and analysis code *as* an R package (`BaBA`'s tracked-animal datasets and behaviour-classification functions, for instance) versus a repository that happens to bundle a vendored copy of someone else's general-purpose package alongside the study's own files (confirmed against `MarshallLab/MGDrivE`, a general-purpose mosquito gene-drive simulation package whose paper-specific fork nests the vendored package one level deep, with the paper's own `Examples/` scripts and data sitting as siblings at the repository root). The corrected rule only excludes a root-level package's files when nothing classifiable as real data or code survives outside it (checked with `data_classify_files()`, the same rules-based classifier `data_check` itself uses, so "real content" means the same thing everywhere in the pipeline); a package detected in a nested subfolder — the vendored-dependency shape — is still always excluded, since by construction there is always something else in the repository for a nested package to sit alongside. Reapplying this corrected rule to the 38 repositories flagged by a corpus-wide scan for the exclusion's symptom (a repository whose only surviving files, after the old exclusion ran, were scaffolding) resolved `r 16 - cc(cooper_right_causes$code_archived, "r_package_source_excluded")` of the 16 confirmed cases; `r cc(cooper_right_causes$code_archived, "r_package_source_excluded")` remain flagged, but for an unrelated, pre-existing reason — a handful of these repositories' cached downloads never retrieved the package's `R/` source directory at all (a fetch gap, not an exclusion-logic problem), so the corrected rule correctly finds nothing outside the package to preserve because nothing outside the package was ever downloaded in the first place. That fetch gap is a separate, still-open limitation, tracked apart from the exclusion fix itself.

### Is any data available at all?
