Three confirmed false-positive mechanisms were fixed: (1) a single-segment string beginning with `/` (e.g. `self.fetch('/login')` in a vendored web-app test suite, `github.com_ccrisan_motioneye/tests/test_handlers/test_login.py`) is an HTTP route, not a filesystem path — 322 of 4,182 originally matched strings were 6 characters or fewer, a class dominated by exactly this pattern; the regex's bare-`/`-prefixed branch now requires a second `/`-separated segment before matching, which a real absolute path (e.g. `/Users/name`) always has and a bare route never does. (2) An all-digit UNC "host" is a `sub()`/`gsub()` regex backreference string, not a network path — confirmed twice in real code: `osf.io_5fter/IDcallR_sameN_withIDcallPP.R` line 183, `sub('group (\d+)_(\d+)', "\2\1", colnames(clupo))`, where `"\2\1"` was matched as `\\host\share` because a bare digit satisfied the old hostname character class; and a second, independent instance in a Pyrenees-mapping script's `gsub('(.{1,10})(\s|$)', '\1\n', ...)` call, matched for the same reason. The UNC branch's hostname character class now requires at least one letter, which excludes both confirmed cases without excluding any real hostname (no genuine UNC host is all-digit-and-punctuation with no letter at all). (3) The pattern's own pre-existing docstring already flagged a known risk — a variable-built path like `paste0(dir, '/file.csv')` triggering a false match on the literal fragment — and this was confirmed for real: `github.com_YvesBas_Tadarida-C/Sonotypes/write_tabase3HF_Sonotype.R` line 40, `list.files(paste(ListDate[[i]],"/eti",sep=""), ...)`, where `"/eti"` is a relative fragment concatenated onto a loop variable. This third mechanism is addressed by the same "require a second path segment" fix as (1), since `/eti` is itself single-segment. A fourth mechanism, confirmed but **not fixed**: a Python string built by `+`-concatenation from a relative literal (`'data\\' + tile_name + '\\run\\' + model_name + ...`, from a Zenodo-hosted `model_test.py`) is a relative path whose middle segments (`\run\`, `\output\tile\`) still match the UNC branch on their own; no fully static regex-only fix exists for this case, since it would require tracking whether the enclosing expression is a string concatenation starting with a relative literal, which is beyond what a line-based regex can determine. Of the true positives sampled for comparison, 15 of 15 further-checked "real username-shaped" matches (e.g. `C:/Users/reddin/Documents/...`, `/Users/farrer/Dropbox/...`, `/home/michael/Dropbox/...`) were confirmed genuine, machine-specific absolute paths — the large majority of this check's flags are correct.

**`setwd()` calls — no false positives found in this corpus; one confirmed-but-unobserved risk noted.** All 194 distinct `setwd()` call strings found across the sampled files are genuine, live, executable calls, including calls whose argument is itself relative or dynamic (`setwd("./data")`, `setwd(dir)`, `setwd(tempdir())`) — these correctly count as flags under this check's own stated rule, since the anti-pattern being flagged is changing the working directory at all, not specifically a hardcoded absolute-path argument. A latent false-positive mechanism was confirmed by construction (a synthetic test, not a real corpus case): `code_setwd()` has no awareness of string-literal context, so a line like `message("Please run setwd(your_path) before continuing")` would be matched as if it were a live call. Scanning all 194 real call strings in the corpus for instructional-text markers ("please," "before," "instructions," "note:") found zero real occurrences of this pattern — a real, demonstrated risk with no confirmed instance in this corpus, and left unfixed for that reason, though `code_setwd()` could straightforwardly reuse the same quote-context-tracking logic already implemented for `.code_strip_inline_comment()` if a future corpus surfaces a real case.

**Comment density — a Python-specific docstring signal added (not a bug fix).** `code_remove_comments()`'s Python branch deliberately never treats a triple-quoted string as a comment, since doing so would also destroy real docstrings (themselves ordinary string literals, syntactically). The consequence, quantified directly: of 280 zero-comment-flagged Python files in the corpus, 200 (71.4%) contain at least one complete triple-quoted docstring block — real documentation that the mechanical `#`-only comment count cannot see, and so reports as "0% comments" regardless. Five were read directly to confirm these are genuine module/function docstrings rather than incidental triple-quoted data, e.g. `model_runs.py`'s `"""Filters for Model Runs."""` and `features.py`'s 16 separate triple-quote markers (8 docstrings) opening with `"""API functions to interact with feature names."""`. This is a deliberate, correctly-reasoned design choice in `code_remove_comments()`, not a bug — stripping docstrings to count them as comments would also delete them from every downstream check that reads code text — so the fix made is additive rather than corrective: a new function, `.code_has_docstring()`, detects whether a file contains at least one complete triple-quoted block, and `code_line_stats()` now returns this as a separate `has_docstring` field (`NA` for every non-Python language) alongside the unchanged `percent_comments` metric. `inst/modules/code_check.R`'s report text now adds an explanatory note whenever a zero-comment Python file in fact has a docstring, so a reader is told the file is documented via docstrings rather than concluding it has no documentation at all.

**Scattered library/import lines — Python import-anchor tightened (fixed).** `code_library_lines()` (`R/code_check.R`) previously anchored its Python import-detection regex on the bare keyword plus a following word (`^\s*(import|from)\s+[A-Za-z_.]`), with no requirement that the rest of the line actually form a valid import statement. Because Python's comment-removal never strips triple-quoted strings (the same mechanism behind the comment-density finding immediately above), docstring *prose* that happens to start with "from " or "import " survives into this scan and was matched as if it were a real import line. Concrete, exact example: `github.com_openvinotoolkit_cvat/site/process_sdk_docs.py`, line 213, inside a docstring spanning lines 211–214 — the prose sentence "        from the generated model and api descriptions." was matched as an import line at line 154 of the comment-stripped text, while the file's 10 real imports are all genuinely contiguous at lines 1–10; the spurious match alone widened the reported gap between imports to 144 lines, crossing the "scattered" threshold (more than 3 non-comment lines between library statements) on a file whose real imports are, in fact, perfectly grouped. Quantified across all 525 Python files flagged as scattered in the corpus: 155 (29.5%) have at least one spurious, non-import match of this kind; of those, 68 (13.0% of all 525 flagged files) would no longer be flagged as scattered at all once the spurious matches are excluded — pure false positives caused entirely by this mechanism (the remaining 87 files with a spurious match are still genuinely scattered even after excluding it). R showed essentially no equivalent problem in a 60-file sample (the one apparent candidate, on manual inspection, was a genuine conditional `require()` call, not a false positive — R's regex requires an opening parenthesis directly after the keyword, structurally harder to spuriously trigger than Python's bare whitespace-plus-word anchor). Fix: the Python pattern now requires the full import shape rather than just the leading keyword — a `from` line must also contain its own `import` keyword later on the same line (`^\s*from\s+[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*\s+import\s`), and a bare `import` line must be followed by a comma-separated identifier list with an optional `as name` and nothing else (`^\s*import\s+[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*(\s*,\s*[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*)*(\s+as\s+\w+)?\s*$`) — verified against the docstring false-positive example above (now correctly unmatched) and against every real import shape found in the corpus sample, including multi-line `from x import (a, b, c)` continuations (matched on their opening line) and indented imports, with no loss of any real detection.

**Status of the fixes in this appendix.** All Metacheck fixes described in A.1 and A.3 (nine in total: #378, #379, #380, #383, both causes of #384, and the five `code_check` fixes from the systematic validation) have been committed to `scienceverse/metacheck`'s `repocheck_improvements` branch (pull request #385) and are covered by the package's automated test suite (463 tests passing at time of writing, 0 failures, 3 pre-existing skips unrelated to these changes). The sixth fix described above (the comparison script's missing-repository default) is not a Metacheck fix and has been committed instead to this project's own `code_data_preparation/03_recreate_cooper_columns.R`, in the `cooper_validation_metacheck` repository. The one defect identified but not yet fixed (`code_read()`'s crash on an empty file, A.2) and the two `code_file_refs()` limitations noted but not yet fixed (A.3) remain open. The further full corpus rerun incorporating the five A.3 fixes, planned when this appendix was first written, has since been performed (confirmed directly: the current corpus run's `code_check` output carries the `has_docstring` field A.3's docstring fix introduces, which cannot exist in a pre-fix run) — the numbers reported in "Results you get for free alongside Metacheck" above reflect that post-fix corpus, not the pre-fix state described earlier in this sentence's original drafting. This was a distinct item from the rerun described in Appendix A.5 below, which re-checked only the papers with a remaining disagreement (not the full corpus) and tested a different set of fixes (Zenodo reliability, repository-platform coverage, and rate-limit handling), not the five A.3 `code_check` fixes.

## A.4 A repository excluded from processing by file count

During the corpus rerun incorporating the A.3 fixes, one paper's data repository — Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.3971689, SAPFLUXNET (a global database of sap flow measurements: 202 datasets from 121 locations, sap flow and environmental time series for 2,714 individual plants) — was found to hold approximately 4,000 individual files. Downloading and, in particular, `data_check`'s per-file classification and full-content read of every one of those files (`data_check_head(..., n_rows = Inf)`, by design, since several of `data_check`'s validation checks need the complete dataset rather than a sample) took several hours and multiple gigabytes of memory for this single paper, out of 1,861 in the corpus, before the run was stopped.

This exposed a real gap in Metacheck: `download_repo_files()` already gates a repository outright by total byte size (`max_download_size`) or per-file byte size (`max_file_size`), but had no gate on file *count* — a repository holding thousands of individually small files was not caught by either existing cap. A new parameter, `max_files_per_repo` (`R/repo-download.R`, threaded through `data_check()` and `code_check()`), gates a repository by file count alone, using the same refusal/reporting mechanism as the existing size caps. This has been committed to the `repocheck_improvements` branch alongside a regression test, and the corpus rerun was configured with `max_files_per_repo = 1000`.

Under this cap, the SAPFLUXNET repository is refused outright rather than downloaded, so this one paper's `data_check`/`code_check` results are incomplete (no files analysed for it) in the corpus run reported in this manuscript. This is a deliberate, scale-driven exclusion of a single outlier repository, not a defect in how that paper's data was assessed — the cap exists specifically so that one exceptionally large repository cannot block or degrade processing of the other 1,860 papers in the corpus. Revisiting this one paper's repository with a raised or absent cap, as a separate, deliberate pass, remains an open option.

## A.5 A targeted rerun on every remaining disagreement, after further platform-detection and reliability fixes

After Appendix A.1–A.4's fixes and the resulting full corpus rerun, every remaining disagreement between Metacheck and Cooper et al.'s coding (991 rows across 989 papers, the same set individually adjudicated for the Empirical Comparison above) was re-checked a further time against Metacheck as it stood after seven more commits landed on `scienceverse/metacheck`'s `dev` branch: two fixing crashes and false negatives in Metacheck's Zenodo integration, three widening which repository *platforms* `repo_check` can locate a repository on at all (targeting "repository not detected," the single largest recurring disagreement cause identified in the original review — see "The five recurring causes" above), and two fixing a rate-limit reliability defect surfaced live during this rerun itself. Rather than reprocess the full 1,861-paper corpus, only the 989 papers with at least one open disagreement were rerun, one paper at a time (so that a single paper's slow host response could not block any other), reusing the shared on-disk repository-file cache from the original corpus run so that a repository already fetched and unchanged cost no new download.

**Zenodo reliability.** Two fixes addressed real crashes and false negatives in Metacheck's Zenodo integration, confirmed against Zenodo records already present in this corpus. `online()`, the function `repo_check` calls to confirm a host is reachable before querying it, treated a single transient DNS lookup miss as "Zenodo is offline" and abandoned that paper's entire Zenodo retrieval rather than retrying; it now retries. Separately, a JSON metadata field arriving as a length-zero value (an empty array) rather than `NULL` defeated the `%||%` operator used throughout Metacheck's metadata-extraction code (which only guards against `NULL`, not length-zero), producing a `data.frame()` "arguments imply differing number of rows" error that was silently swallowed inside a `tryCatch`, discarding the whole record; a new `%empty_or%` operator, applied everywhere the same gap existed (Dataverse, Dryad, DSpace7, Figshare, GitHub, GitLab, OSF, PsychArchives, and ReShare, not just Zenodo), closes this. A further, closely related pair of crashes was found and fixed the same way: a Zenodo record Metacheck could not read at all previously returned a `data.frame()` with only `zenodo_id`/`error` columns, so a paper whose every Zenodo record was unreadable produced a metadata table with no `doi`/`license` columns at all, which crashed `repo_check()`'s own Zenodo-metadata-extraction step for that paper the same "differing number of rows" way; and a `repo_url` arriving as a list column (rather than a plain character vector) could silently explode `data.frame(zenodo_url = <list>)` into one column per list element instead of the expected single column. Both are now guarded.

**Repository platform coverage.** Three commits substantially widened the set of hosts Metacheck's `repo_check` can locate a repository on at all, directly targeting the "repository not detected" cause responsible for the largest share of the original disagreement (see "The five recurring causes" above, which named DataSTORRE, DIGITAL.CSIC, AADC, SRA/GenBank, KNB, Neotoma, CIRAD Dataverse, and ForestPlots.net as example platforms with no backend at the time). Mendeley Data (detected via `10.17632/` DOIs and `data.mendeley.com` URLs, queried through the public, unauthenticated `data.mendeley.com/public-api/datasets/<id>` endpoint) and DataONE (a federation of independently-run repositories rather than one hosted service; four member nodes verified live and wired in — Arctic Data Center, KNB, Taiwan Forestry Research Institute, and the Smithsonian Tropical Data Portal, each mounting the same underlying REST API at a different base path) were added as new platforms entirely. Separately, Dataverse's recognised-installation list was expanded from 50 to 121 hosts, 16 institutional Figshare white-label front ends were added, and DSpace support was generalized from PsychArchives specifically to any host running the same legacy (≤6) API (5 more verified live) plus a new implementation covering 64 DSpace 7 installations (e.g. Cornell's eCommons, Georgia Tech's Digital Repository, ETH Zurich's Research Collection) — every one of these 121 + 16 + 5 + 64 hosts confirmed live via its own version/info endpoint before being added, not merely listed from a registry. A further, smaller fix excludes an R package's own source tree (`DESCRIPTION`/`NAMESPACE`/its `R/`/`man/`/`tests/` subdirectories) from a repository's data/code file listing, on the reasoning that reusable software infrastructure bundled alongside a study's own materials is not itself the study's data or analysis code and should not inflate `files_n`/`files_code` or appear in downstream reports.

**A reliability defect found live during this rerun.** While this rerun was in progress, a single paper stalled repeatedly at the same point across two separate attempts: `zip_peek()`'s HEAD request and its Range-request follow-up (`.http_range_tail()`, `R/zip-peek.R`), used to read a remote zip archive's file listing without downloading it, each independently hit Zenodo's rate limit and each, independently, paid the full announced wait for the host's confirmed reset — three consecutive confirmed-rate-limit waits back to back for what was, from Zenodo's own side, a single rate-limit window, since neither request had any way to know the other had already discovered and waited out the same limit. (The rate-limit-wait message itself was also, at the same time, made to name the specific host responsible — Zenodo, Dryad, GitHub, or GitLab, the only hosts that expose a machine-readable reset time — rather than reporting only "the host's own reset," a smaller, secondary fix made in the course of diagnosing this one.) Fix: a session-scoped record of the last confirmed rate-limit reset per host, written the first time any request discovers one and consulted by every subsequent request to that host before it is even sent, so a host already known to be rate-limited waits out only the genuinely remaining time once, rather than every independent request rediscovering the identical window from a fresh 429. Verified with new regression tests covering the record/lookup logic directly (round-tripping a wait, keeping the later of two recorded resets, clearing an expired window, and the pre-flight wait actually sleeping the correct duration) and confirmed live: the same paper that previously stalled for over 40 minutes across three stacked waits resolved in roughly 3 minutes with zero confirmed-rate-limit waits after the fix, the remaining time attributable to Zenodo's own server-side response latency for that specific record (confirmed independently: a single isolated request to the same record, made outside Metacheck entirely, itself took 30 seconds and returned a 504 on a second attempt).

**Results of the rerun.** Across the 1,532 individual construct-level disagreements re-checked (989 papers × up to 7 constructs each, matching however many constructs a given paper had originally disagreed on), 76.8% (1,176 of 1,532) are now resolved — Metacheck's fresh result agrees with Cooper et al.'s original human coding where it did not before — with 348 still disagreeing and 1 now returning a value that could not be classified as agreeing or disagreeing (`data_license`, a repository whose licence field this rerun could not read for reasons not yet diagnosed). By construct: `any_readme` 548/625 resolved (87.7%), `data_availability` 339/424 (80.0%), `code_archived` 252/360 (70.0%), `data_archive` 12/56 (21.4%, evaluated by set membership — a paper's platform coded by Cooper now appearing among Metacheck's own, possibly multi-platform, detected set, since a paper can genuinely link more than one repository), `data_license` 16/57 (28.1%), `data_download` 9/9 (100%), and `code_download` 0/1 (the sole remaining `code_download` disagreement in this corpus). The comparatively modest improvement in `data_archive` and `data_license` is consistent with the original review's own finding that these two constructs' disagreement was, unlike `data_availability`/`code_archived`/`any_readme`, not dominated by the repository-detection cause these fixes targeted (`data_license`'s largest cause was, per "Opposite direction" above, cases where Metacheck was already right and Cooper's own coding had missed a real licence field) — a fix aimed at finding more repositories naturally does less for a construct whose disagreement was rarely about a missing repository in the first place. This rerun's full row-level detail (every paper, every re-checked construct, the value before and after, and whether it resolved) is recorded in `cooper_validation_metacheck/manuscript/data/rerun_disagreements_comparison.csv`, produced by `rerun_disagreements.R`; the underlying per-paper `repo_check`/`data_check`/`code_check` results are cached per paper in `data/rerun_batches/` for inspection or a further rerun without recomputing what has not changed.

**Checking the rest of the corpus for regressions.** This rerun was scoped to the 989 previously-disagreeing papers only — a deliberate choice at the time, to get a fast answer to "did these fixes help" without the cost of a full 1,861-paper rerun (see the rerun's own header comment for the reasoning). That scoping left one real question open: none of these seven fixes were written to only affect a disagreeing paper, so it remained possible that a fix which resolved one paper's disagreement had, in a different paper that already agreed with Cooper et al., turned a correct result into an incorrect one — most plausibly the R-package-source-tree exclusion (if a paper's own analysis code happens to be organised as an R package) or the expanded Dataverse/Figshare/DSpace/Mendeley/DataONE host recognition (a newly-recognised host matching something that should not have counted). This was checked directly: the remaining 868 papers (every paper not in the 989-paper disagreement set) were also rerun, using the identical per-paper, resumable approach, and the full corpus's `cooper_vs_recreated.RData`/disagreement worklist were then rebuilt from the combined result (all 1,861 papers) rather than just the 989. At the level of aggregate agreement rates, this full-corpus check was reassuring: the three constructs this comparison's own disagreement was concentrated in — `data_availability`, `code_archived`, `any_readme` — all showed a higher, not lower, agreement rate once the previously-agreeing papers were included, and `data_download`/`code_download` (both already above 99%) moved by less than a percentage point in either direction. But an aggregate rate rising is consistent with a handful of individual papers having genuinely regressed, provided enough *other* papers improved to more than offset them — and that is exactly what the case-by-case review below found.

**A confirmed regression, found and fixed within this same cycle.** The suspicion named above turned out to be correct: the R-package-source-tree exclusion did break papers it should not have touched. The exclusion was written to detect an R package's fingerprint (a `DESCRIPTION` and `NAMESPACE` file in the same folder) and drop that folder's contents — the package's `R/`, `man/`, `tests/`, `vignettes/`, `data/`, `inst/`, and `src/` subdirectories — from a repository's file listing entirely, on the reasoning that a bundled, reusable software dependency is not itself a study's data or analysis code. That reasoning holds when the package is a genuine dependency vendored alongside a study's own files, but it does not hold when the paper's *own* contribution — its data, its analysis code, or both — is itself packaged and distributed as an installable R package, a common practice in ecological/evolutionary methods work. In that case the exclusion strips the paper's own materials, leaving nothing behind: `repo_check`'s listing for the affected repository showed only packaging scaffolding (`.Rbuildignore`, `.gitignore`, `NEWS.md`, `README.md`, `cran-comments.md`, a bare `.Rproj` file), with the package's real `R/` source — and, for packages that bundle their own example or study data under `data/`, the actual dataset — entirely absent.

A corpus-wide scan for this exact symptom (a repository whose only surviving files, after the exclusion ran, were scaffolding, with zero files classified as data or code) surfaced candidates across the full 1,861-paper corpus, each individually verified against the repository's real GitHub listing (via `gh api`) or Dryad/Zenodo record before being counted: 16 confirmed true instances (`RevGadgets`, `BaBA`, `m2b`, `RRPP`, `actel`, `scampr`, `MINOTAUR`, `LadderFuelsR`, `biomonitoR`, `EcoEnsemble`, `fossilsim`, `frair`, `tRophicPosition`, `sabinaNSDM`, `bef`, and `phylomice`), plus several candidates from the same scan that turned out to be unrelated causes once checked directly (a repository with no `DESCRIPTION`/`NAMESPACE` at all, and several Dryad/Zenodo-hosted papers whose `code_archived` disagreement traced to an unconnected, pre-existing detection gap — code cited in a journal's own Supporting Information, or a repository never located by `repo_check` at all). Two confirmed cases (`BaBA`, a GitHub-hosted barrier-behaviour-analysis package whose `data/` folder holds the actual tracked-animal datasets for its own paper, and `MGDrivE`, a general-purpose mosquito gene-drive simulation package vendored inside a study-specific fork) between them illustrated the structural distinction the fix needed to draw: `BaBA`'s package sits at its repository's root with nothing else present — the package *is* the deposit, so nothing should be excluded — while `MGDrivE`'s vendored copy is nested one level deep inside the fork, with the study's own `Examples/` scripts and data sitting as real, undisputed siblings at the repository root.

The corrected rule preserves the original exclusion's logic for a nested package (still always excluded, since a nested package by construction always has something else in the repository for it to sit alongside) but adds one check for a package detected at a repository's *root*: before excluding it, check whether anything outside the package folder classifies as real data or code, using `data_classify_files()` — the same rules-based classifier `data_check` itself uses elsewhere in the pipeline, rather than a separate, bespoke list of what counts as "real content." If nothing does, the package is not excluded at all, since there is no "outside" for the study's own materials to live in. One implementation detail required a second pass: an RStudio project marker file (`*.Rproj`) classifies as `"code"` under `data_classify_files()` purely by its file extension, which would have wrongly counted as "real content survives" for every package that ships one (nearly all of them) — an RStudio project file is packaging configuration, not an analysis script, so it is excluded from this specific check. The fix was verified against two new regression tests (a root-level package with nothing else present, confirming it is no longer excluded, and a nested vendored package alongside real sibling content, confirming the vendored files are still excluded while the sibling content survives) alongside the existing test suite, then reapplied to the 38 papers the corpus-wide scan had flagged.

Reapplying the corrected exclusion resolved `r 16 - cc(cooper_right_causes$code_archived, "r_package_source_excluded")` of the 16 confirmed cases outright. The remaining `r cc(cooper_right_causes$code_archived, "r_package_source_excluded")` continue to show `code_archived` disagreement, but for a distinct and unrelated reason discovered while reprocessing them: their cached downloaded files never included the package's `R/` source directory in the first place — only packaging scaffolding was ever fetched from the host — so the corrected exclusion logic correctly finds nothing outside the (never-fully-downloaded) package to preserve, because nothing beyond scaffolding was ever retrieved. This is a fetch-completeness gap, not an exclusion-logic problem, and is not further diagnosed here; it is recorded as a separate, still-open limitation rather than folded into a claim about the exclusion fix's own effectiveness. Two of the 16, `phylomice` and `morton` — cases surfaced by the same corpus-wide scan but outside the original 13-paper set found during the initial regression check — resolved to, respectively, `METACHECK_RIGHT` (`phylomice`'s six R source files are a genuine methods contribution the paper's own text never explicitly claims as "archived code," but which Metacheck is nonetheless correct to report) and `COOPER_RIGHT` (`morton`'s 37 R source files are unambiguously this paper's own phylogenetic-analysis code, which Cooper et al.'s coders had missed).

## A.6 A systematic platform-coverage audit, three further metacheck fixes, and a complete categorization of every remaining repository-detection disagreement

A sixth round of work started from a single case the previous rounds had not caught: a paper citing a Dataverse installation (`borealisdata.ca`, Borealis, the Canadian national repository) under a DOI prefix Appendix A.5's Dataverse allowlist did not recognise. Tracing why surfaced a systemic problem in how that allowlist had been built, and prompted a full re-audit of every remaining "repository not detected" disagreement in the corpus rather than a single-paper patch.

**A systemic under-sampling bug in the Dataverse DOI-prefix allowlist.** Appendix A.5's per-host Dataverse DOI-prefix allowlist (`.dataverse_doi_prefix_hosts()`) was originally built by sampling the first 25 DOIs DataCite's search API returned for each host — a sample, not a census. This badly under-counted any host with more than 25 real DOIs registered, which turned out to be the majority of the 121 known hosts; `borealisdata.ca` alone has minted DOIs under six distinct prefixes, of which the original allowlist recorded only one. Rebuilding the allowlist using DataCite's facet aggregation (`disable-facets=false` on its `/dois` search, which returns every distinct prefix in use for a host, with its real count, in one request rather than a sample) found 100 distinct prefixes across the same 87 hosts, not 87 — including a second Harvard Dataverse prefix (`10.26300`, alongside the dominant `10.7910`) that the original sample had also missed. Verified live before and after: the DOI that surfaced this bug (`10.7939/DVN/M6Q2PE`, Borealis) now resolves correctly, and the second Harvard prefix now resolves to `dataverse.harvard.edu`. This was reported and merged upstream as scienceverse/metacheck#410.

**Two further platform-coverage gaps found and fixed the same way.** `.figshare_id()` did not recognise a Figshare article URL with no resource-type segment (`figshare.com/articles/<slug>/<id>`, as opposed to `figshare.com/articles/dataset/<slug>/<id>`) — an older, still-current URL shape (confirmed live against a real corpus citation) that `figshare_links()` already detected as a Figshare link but could not resolve to a usable article id, so `repo_check` never actually queried it (scienceverse/metacheck#412). Separately, `dataone_links()` had no entry for `data.piscoweb.org` (PISCO, a UC Santa Barbara-run DataONE member node), and `.dataone_pid()`'s bare-DOI regex could not handle a DOI suffix containing a further slash — PISCO's own DOI shape (`10.6085/AA/<id>`) — so this platform's citations, while real DataONE member-node DOIs, were invisible end to end. Both fixed and merged as scienceverse/metacheck#414, which also added 29 further institutional Figshare instances (28 found by searching DataCite's client registry for "figshare" in the client name, plus Monash University's `bridges.monash.edu`, found separately since its DataCite client is registered under the institution's own name) — each confirmed live, the same way as every host already in `.figshare_vanity_hosts()`, to answer Figshare's own single-page-app shell rather than a real API response, and each institutional DOI prefix confirmed live to resolve to that exact host before being added.

**Two matching bugs in this project's own comparison code, not in Metacheck.** `03_recreate_cooper_columns.R`'s `.repo_url_platform()` — the function that labels which platform `mc_data_archive` reports for a paper — had a Dryad branch that only matched the single most common DOI prefix (`10.5061`), and a Figshare branch that only matched the literal `figshare.com`/`10.6084` domain and prefix, missing every one of the alternate Dryad prefixes and institutional Figshare instances Metacheck itself already recognised after the fixes above. The practical effect was a paper whose repository *was* now correctly found and retrieved still showing a `data_archive` disagreement, because the label fell through to the generic "Other repo/database" instead of naming the real platform. Both branches were rewritten to read directly from Metacheck's own `.dryad_doi_prefixes()`/`.figshare_vanity_hosts()`/`.figshare_doi_prefix_hosts()` rather than duplicating either list by hand, so this classification cannot drift out of sync with what Metacheck itself recognises again.

**Reprocessing every paper these fixes could plausibly affect.** Rather than assume the fixes above were the only remaining cause of repository-detection disagreement, every "repository not detected" comment still open in the worklist (351 individual (paper, column) disagreements across 233 papers, after excluding platforms already confirmed unsupported for an unrelated reason) was checked again: first narrowed locally, with no network calls, to the papers whose cited DOI prefix genuinely matched one of the platforms just fixed (27 candidates, after excluding two DOI prefixes that coincidentally collide with an unrelated platform's registered prefix in DataCite's own data — `10.6084`, Figshare's own prefix, and `10.17617`, Edmond's — neither of which any fix above touched), then live-verified one at a time. Of those 27, 13 were genuinely resolved by the fixes above; the remaining 14 were not — some detect the citation correctly but the dataset is embargoed or restricted at the source (confirmed via the repository's own API returning an explicit "cannot be viewed" message, not a Metacheck-side failure), and a few still do not detect the citation at all, for reasons unrelated to any fix in this round. A further, separately-run check across every remaining "never located" comment surfaced one exact repeat of Appendix A.1's original zip-peek limitation on a much larger scale (24 papers whose Zenodo/Figshare/Dataverse archive was never successfully peeked during an earlier corpus build, confirmed live, unmodified, to peek correctly today — a stale corpus row in every one of the 24, not a code defect). A further paper, initially suspected to be a second such stale row (its earlier 4TU fetch crash was already fixed in Appendix A.1 and appeared simply never rerun since), was checked directly against `rerun_disagreements_comparison.csv`'s own before/after values and found to still disagree after being rerun — the 4TU fetch failure was not, in fact, resolved. A later, more thorough recheck (Appendix A.9) traced the actual cause: 4TU is a genuinely supported platform, but its DOI-embedded identifier does not match the numeric article ID 4TU's own API requires, a distinct, still-open defect from the one Appendix A.1 fixed. This paper is accordingly counted as `SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_BUG`, not `UNSUPPORTED_REPO`, in Appendix A.9's categorization. All resolved candidates from this round were rerun end to end (`repo_check`, `data_check`, `code_check`) and patched into the corpus; none of this round's rerunning touched a paper outside the specific set each check identified, so no regression check across the unaffected remainder of the corpus was needed the way Appendix A.5's broader platform-coverage changes required.

## A.7 A full-corpus `reproducibility_check` run: method, outputs, reasons for non-reproducibility, and suggested improvements to Metacheck

A seventh round of work ran Metacheck's `reproducibility_check` module — a module distinct from `repo_check`/`data_check`/`code_check` (the three modules the rest of this manuscript is about) in that it does not merely detect and classify a paper's shared data and code, but actually **executes** the paper's own downloaded code against the paper's own shared data, inside an isolated sandbox, and checks whether the statistical results the code produces match what the paper itself reports in its text. This appendix documents the method, every output file this run produced, a full breakdown of why papers were and were not reproducible, four new Metacheck defects this run surfaced (all reported upstream, two confirmed fixed on `dev` before this appendix was written), and a set of concrete suggestions for further improving `reproducibility_check` itself.

### A.7.1 Method

`reproducibility_check(paper, execute = TRUE, sandbox = "docker", install_missing = TRUE, timeout = 3000, cache = TRUE, workers = 5, results_dir = ...)` was run once per paper across the full 1,861-paper corpus. For each paper with at least one code file, the module: (1) reuses `code_check`'s dependency extraction and `psychds_check`'s path-rewrite plan to materialise a throwaway copy of the paper's own Psych-DS-layout data and code; (2) installs the paper's declared package dependencies (CRAN, GitHub, or URL sources) into a throwaway library inside a Docker container, starting from the pre-built `ghcr.io/scienceverse/metacheck_r:latest` image (roughly 750 of the most common packages found across a prior corpus scan already installed, so most papers skip most of the install step); (3) runs each of the paper's scripts, in an automatically-derived dependency order, each in its own `docker run --network none --read-only --user <non-root>` invocation — network disabled and the filesystem read-only outside the materialised sandbox, a genuine containment boundary for running downloaded, unvetted third-party code, unlike the module's alternative `sandbox = "process"` backend (a bare `callr` subprocess, which isolates a crash but not the filesystem or network); and (4) extracts any statistical output the executed scripts printed to the console and compares it against the paper's own reported results (`match_reported_output()`), recording how many of the paper's own reported test statistics the executed code actually reproduced.

`workers = 5` runs up to five papers' Docker containers concurrently rather than one at a time, a feature added to Metacheck (`dev` branch, version 0.3.1) specifically to make a corpus-scale run practical; each concurrent container is automatically capped to `1/workers` of the host's CPU and memory, so five containers running at once cannot collectively exceed what the host machine has. `results_dir` writes each paper's complete result to its own file the moment that paper finishes, independent of any outer batch boundary, so a run interrupted partway through does not lose the papers that already completed. A dedicated wrapper script (`reproducibility_check/run_reproducibility_check.R`, `cooper-bes-validation-manuscript` repository) drives the corpus-wide call, installing Metacheck fresh from `scienceverse/metacheck`'s `dev` branch at the start of every run (never a locally vendored copy, so the run always reflects the current state of the package's own repository) and writing one checkpoint file per outer batch so a killed or crashed run can resume from the last completed batch rather than restarting from scratch.

### A.7.2 Outputs stored

The run produced the following files, all in `cooper-bes-validation-manuscript/data/` unless noted:

- **`reproducibility_check_results_execute.RData`** — the final, combined result for all 1,861 papers: an `out` object with `out$results$table` (4,394 rows, one row per script attempted across every code-bearing paper: `paper_id`, `file_name`, `outcome`, `error_type`, `undefined_var`, `not_runnable_reason`, `runnable`, `parses`, `run_order`, `paths_rewritten`, `paths_ambiguous`, `setwd_removed`, `unresolved_inputs`, `reads`, `writes`) and `out$results$summary_table` (1,861 rows, one row per paper: `paper_id`, `repro_code_n`, `repro_runnable`, `repro_missing_inputs`, `repro_deps`, `repro_tests_reported`, `repro_tests_matched`, `repro_ran_ok`). This is the file the numbers below are computed from.
- **`data/batches/`** — one `.RData` checkpoint file per outer batch processed during the run (batch-size-tagged in its filename, so a checkpoint from one `--batch-size` setting is never mistaken for one from another), and, under `data/batches/worker_results/`, one `.rds` file per paper (`capture_module_tables()`'s own per-paper checkpoint format), the finer-grained safety net `results_dir` provides underneath the outer batch files.
- **`reproducibility_check_infra_rerun.RData`** and **`reproducibility_check_13384_solo_rerun.RData`** — two small, targeted follow-up runs (below), covering respectively the 16 papers whose first-pass result was an infrastructure failure rather than a genuine check, and one paper rerun alone (no concurrency) after crashing twice under `workers = 5`.
- **`reproducibility_check_execute_warnings.log`** — every R warning raised during the run, forwarded here as it happened (R's own default non-interactive behaviour silently drops all but the first 50 warnings of a session, which a run this size would exceed many times over).
- Two standalone wrapper scripts alongside the main run script, both in `reproducibility_check/`: `rerun_infra_failures.R` (the 16-paper targeted rerun) and `rerun_single_paper.R` (the one-paper, no-concurrency rerun).

### A.7.3 Scope: which papers had code to check at all

Of the 1,861 papers in the corpus, 343 (18.4%) had at least one code file for `reproducibility_check` to attempt (`repro_code_n > 0`); the remaining 1,517 (81.5%) had none, and are not further discussed in this section, since there is nothing for the module to execute — this is the same "does the paper share any code" question `code_check`/`repo_check` already answer elsewhere in this manuscript, not a new finding. One paper (10\_1111\_2041\_210x\_13384) has no genuine `repro_code_n` value at all (`NA`); this is the one paper described in A.7.5 below whose check was manually aborted rather than completed.

**Note on this count.** This section's original run (below) found code for 334 papers. Appendix A.8 describes three further Metacheck fixes (`zip_peek()` failing on S3-backed hosts, its result never persisting across a restart, and a silently discarded download error) that, once applied and the corpus rerun, let `repo_check`/`code_check` correctly find and download a code repository, or a code file inside one, for papers where they previously could not — 98 papers corpus-wide whose available code or data content genuinely changed. Those 98 papers' `reproducibility_check` result was rerun against the same fixed Metacheck version and merged into this section's own combined result; every other code-bearing paper's original result, from before Appendix A.8, is unchanged. 9 of the 98 newly show `repro_code_n > 0` where they previously showed none, bringing the code-bearing total from 334 to 343; `repro_ran_ok` improved for 5 of the 98 rerun papers (from 138 to 154 papers corpus-wide with at least one script that ran without error). The numbers throughout the rest of A.7.3–A.7.4 below reflect this merged, current result.

### A.7.4 Reasons for non-reproducibility: a full breakdown

Across the 343 code-bearing papers, 4,394 individual scripts were attempted (one paper's script count was not resolved; see A.7.5). Their outcomes:

| Outcome | Count | % of 4,394 |
|---|---|---|
| `ran_ok` (executed without error) | 1,993 | 45.4% |
| `errored` (executed, but raised an R error) | 1,879 | 42.8% |
| `skipped_missing_inputs` (an earlier script's output this script needs was never produced or found) | 459 | 10.4% |
| `not_parsed` (the file is not valid R/syntax in its declared language at all) | 49 | 1.1% |
| `timed_out` (still running when the 3,000-second per-script cutoff was reached) | 14 | 0.3% |

**At the paper level**, only 85 of the 343 code-bearing papers (24.8%) had *every one* of their scripts run without error; 136 (39.7%) had *zero* scripts run successfully at all; the remaining 122 (35.6%) had a mix of successful and failed scripts within the same paper.

**Among the 1,879 `errored` scripts** (plus the 14 `timed_out` scripts, grouped in here since both carry an `error_type`), `error_type` breaks down as:

- **637 (33.7%) `undefined_variable`** — the script references a variable, object, or function that was never defined at the point it is used, the classic signature of a script written to be run only as one step within a larger, undocumented pipeline (e.g. an interactive session, or a preceding script the paper's repository does not include or that this run's automatic dependency ordering could not place before it). The single most common such name, by a wide margin, is the pipe operator **`%>%` itself (15 occurrences)** — a script using `%>%` without ever calling `library(magrittr)`, `library(dplyr)`, or (on R versions before 4.1) without the base pipe `|>` available, a specific and mechanically fixable non-reproducibility cause distinct from the rest of this category's more idiosyncratic missing-object cases. `.jinit` (13 occurrences, from `rJava`-dependent packages needing a Java runtime this Docker image does not provide) is the next most common, followed by a long tail of paper-specific object and function names.
- **1,242 (65.6%) `runtime`** — every other kind of R error raised during execution: a missing package the install phase could not provide (see repro_deps below), a file the script expects that a path-rewrite could not correctly relocate, a genuine bug in the paper's own analysis code, or code that assumes an interactive session (see the two concrete cases below).
- **14 (0.7%) `timeout`** — see the 3,000-second cutoff above; a timeout is not itself counted as strong evidence of non-reproducibility (the paper's own analysis may simply be legitimately slow, e.g. a Bayesian model or a large agent-based simulation — several confirmed cases during this run were exactly this), just "did not finish within the budget this run allowed."

Two concrete, directly observed non-reproducibility patterns are worth naming explicitly, since neither is visible in the `error_type` classification above (both were classified `runtime`, and the module does not currently distinguish "this code assumes an interactive terminal" as its own category — see A.7.6's first suggestion): (1) a script calling base R's `read.csv()` with no path argument, which opens an interactive `file.choose()` file-picker dialog — impossible inside a headless, network-disabled container, and a strong signal the paper's own code was never actually run non-interactively even by its own authors; (2) a script calling `rstanarm::launch_shinystan()`, which starts a Shiny web server and blocks waiting for a browser connection that can never arrive in this sandbox — resolved only by the per-script timeout eventually killing it, after up to 3,000 seconds spent doing nothing.

**Missing inputs.** 129 of the 343 code-bearing papers (37.6%) have at least one script whose required input was never produced or found (`repro_missing_inputs > 0`); 417 individual scripts are recorded `not_runnable_reason = "missing_input"`, the largest single `not_runnable_reason` category by a wide margin (68 `parse_error`, 40 `unplaceable` — a script the run-order algorithm could not confidently place in a dependency sequence at all — and 3 `jags_model`, a script that is itself a JAGS model-definition file rather than executable R).

**Dependency installation.** Before running a paper's code, Metacheck must first install the R packages that code declares it needs. 274 of the 343 code-bearing papers (79.9%) declare at least one such package (`repro_deps`, a per-paper count of declared packages — not a count of failures, and not tied to any particular script or file), 3,508 packages in total. The per-package install success/failure counts, the specific packages that failed and how many papers each affected, and the result-matching statistics later in this subsection come from a dedicated extraction against each paper's saved checkpoint report text (`01_run_metacheck/08_extract_reproducibility_detail.R`), which reads each paper's own free-text install-summary sentence and, for result matching, its row-level `match_table`. This extraction was rebuilt for the current, merged 343-paper result; the original script that first built it for the pre-Appendix-A.8 pass was not itself preserved anywhere in this project (see the note further below).

Metacheck's own `summary_table` records only *how many* packages a paper declares (`repro_deps`), not *which* ones failed to install or why — a real limitation this appendix works around below, and A.7.6's second suggestion recommends Metacheck fix directly. This appendix could still recover the failed packages' actual *names*, because each paper's saved checkpoint file also keeps a plain-text summary sentence restating its own install attempt (e.g. "13 succeeded, 9 failed. sf, rgdal, ... were installed. **Failed:** countreg, DTK, ..."); re-reading that sentence for each paper is how the list below was built. 256 of the 265 papers had this sentence in a readable form; the other 9 are a gap in what this appendix could recover, not evidence of anything about those 9 papers' own installs.

One further point, worth stating plainly rather than folding into the numbers above: none of the 361 failed installs were classified by Metacheck as `dependency_unavailable` — its own label for "this package cannot be found anywhere, so this is not really about the paper's own code." Every failure here was instead classified as an ordinary code error, which this appendix takes as license to keep treating a failed install as a real, meaningful cause of non-reproducibility, not something to set aside as merely today's state of the package ecosystem.

The rest of this subsection focuses on the 80 papers identified above: a real install failure, and no script that ran successfully. This is the subset where a failed install is most clearly the reason the paper's code did not run.

**Note on this list.** As with the numbers in A.7.3/A.7.4 above, this list was rebuilt (using this project's own `01_run_metacheck/08_extract_reproducibility_detail.R`, re-parsing each paper's saved checkpoint report text) after Appendix A.8's rerun, since the original extraction script that first built it was not itself preserved anywhere in this project (only its output — `01_run_metacheck/batches/reproducibility_check/pre_a8_reference/` — survived). The rebuilt extraction was checked directly against that surviving output for every package outside Appendix A.8's 98-paper rerun before being trusted: of the 90 packages the original extraction found, 86 have an identical paper count in the rebuild, 2 (`rethinking`, `rJava`) changed by one paper each as a direct, explicable result of the rerun, and 2 (`ascr`, `pgirmess`) no longer appear because the one paper each had failed for moved out of this 76-to-80-paper subset (its code now has at least one successful script, or its failed install no longer applies) — a small, fully accounted-for set of differences, not evidence of a remaining extraction problem.

**Which packages failed to install, for the 80 papers with a failed dependency and zero successful scripts.** Every one of these 80 papers has a `report` field in the saved checkpoint data with a recoverable, itemised list of which specific packages failed. Across those 80 papers, 187 individual failed-install records were recovered, naming 109 distinct packages. Five of those, across several papers, are not genuine package names at all but a further Metacheck defect: `x`, `package`, `not_installed`, `arma`, and `packages.toinstall` were each confirmed absent from CRAN entirely and, on direct inspection of the paper's own repository, are variable names from the paper's *own* install-loop code (e.g. `for (pkg in list.packages) install.packages(pkg)`) that Metacheck's dependency extractor mistook for a literal package name to install — see A.7.5's newly-added fifth defect below.

By far the most common genuine cause is a small cluster of interdependent **spatial/GIS packages**: `sf`, `rgdal`, `rgeos`, `maptools`, `stars`, `ggspatial`, `mapview`, `tmap`, `gdalUtils`, `nngeo`, and `spatial.tools` are not ordinary self-contained R packages but R interfaces to external, non-R system libraries — GDAL (reads/writes geographic file formats), GEOS (geometric operations such as intersections and buffers), and PROJ (coordinate-system transformations) — which must already be installed at the operating-system level before the R package can even compile, let alone load; installing the R package alone is not sufficient. `sf` (22 papers), `rgdal` (17), `maptools` (7), `rgeos` (6), `ggspatial` (4), and `stars` (4), together with the smaller one/two-paper members of the same cluster, account for 68 of the 187 records (36.4%) — consistent with a single shared environment gap (`ghcr.io/scienceverse/metacheck_r:latest` apparently does not have GDAL/GEOS/PROJ installed) rather than 68 independent per-paper causes; see Suggestion 2 below, which recommends closing this gap directly in Metacheck's own Docker image rather than leaving it to recur for every future spatial-analysis paper. The next-largest identifiable cluster is **Bayesian/JAGS modelling**: `rjags` (4 papers), `R2jags` (1), and `INLA` (1) — JAGS is itself a separate, non-R program that must be installed on the system for `rjags` to link against, the same category of gap as the spatial cluster. A `Java`-dependent cluster (`rJava`, 4 papers, matching the `.jinit` `undefined_variable` pattern reported above) similarly requires a system-level Java runtime, not just the R package.

Every other package in the list below failed for exactly one paper each. This appendix cannot say *why* each of these one-off packages failed to install, and one specific possibility this run's own method already rules out for the great majority of them is worth naming directly: Metacheck's `sandbox = "process"` install backend (`repro_install_deps()`) retries a failed live-CRAN install once against the CRAN Archive (a package's last-published version before CRAN removed it) before giving up — but this run used `sandbox = "docker"`, whose install backend (`repro_install_deps_docker()`) does **not** implement this same Archive retry (confirmed directly against its own source; its `via_archive` field is hard-coded `FALSE` for every install, with an explicit comment noting the retry "is not duplicated here"). So a package that failed here only because its current CRAN release could not compile, but whose Archive-held prior version would have installed cleanly, was never given the chance this run — the Archive retry that might have recovered it simply was not attempted, independent of whatever the package's own true availability status is. A handful of names (e.g. `hmRLib`, `poispkgs`, `tiagospackage`) are also plausibly a typo or a private/unpublished package never intended for public installation at all, though this was not individually verified for each. This is a separate, more specific point than this appendix's general scope note below: it is not merely that the *reason* for each one-off failure is unrecorded, but that one entire category of possible reason (an Archive-recoverable package) was structurally never tested for in this run at all.

The full list, package name and number of these 80 papers it failed for (n = 1 except where noted): **sf** (22), **rgdal** (17), **maptools** (7), **rgeos** (6), **ggsn** (4), **ggspatial** (4), **rjags** (4), **rJava** (4), **stars** (4), **phyloseq** (3), **amt** (2), **Biostrings** (2), **dada2** (2), **decontam** (2), **gdalUtils** (2), **glmulti** (2), **mapview** (2), **mcmcplots** (2), **rethinking** (2), **ShortRead** (2), **tmap** (2), adiv, asreml, betalink, brtest, CAST, classecol, CommEcol, countreg, dartR, diveRsity, DTK, embryogrowth, emmeans, evobiR, FancyBaSTA2, fishflux, FRQNT1.Data, GeoLight, GeoLocTools, ggalt, gghalves, ggmosaic, ggordiplots, ggpattern, GISTools, git2r, glmmADMB, gurobi, GVI, hdi, hier.part, hilldiv, hmRLib, InformationValue, INLA, IPMpack, jpeg, lme4, lmerTest, MCMCglmm, microbiome, microclima, NicheMapR, nngeo, odeintr, Orcs, pairwiseAdonis, PAMLr, parameters, PCAviz, performance, performanceEstimation, pez, phylolm, picante, plotrix, prioritizr, purr, R2jags, RAMClustR, Rarefy, razimuth, rgl, rich, RNetLogo, seqRFLP, SGAT, siar, SNPRelate, spatial.tools, spdep, tabulizer, taxotools, tess3r, tidync, tidyverse, TwGeos, units, V.PhyloMaker, vegetarian, viridis, waffle, and weathercan.

**A note on scope for this package list.** This list names which package failed to install, for how many papers, within the 80-paper subset defined above (a genuine install failure, and zero scripts of that paper ran successfully); it is not a claim about why each package failed (a version incompatibility, a missing system library, a compilation failure, genuine current unavailability, or something else) — Metacheck's own `.repro_classify_install_message()` classifier already exists and runs during the install phase, but its per-package `category` output is not retained in this run's paper-level `summary_table`, the same gap A.7.6's second suggestion recommends closing. Nor does this list cover the 82 further papers (162 total with a genuine install failure minus the 80 covered here) that had at least one failed dependency but still had at least one script run successfully — extracting and reporting that broader set's package list, and each package's classified failure reason once Metacheck retains it, is a natural extension of this analysis and is not attempted here.

**Result matching: did the code's own output match what the paper reports?** This is a distinct, further step `reproducibility_check` performs beyond simply running a paper's code: for every paper whose code did produce console output, it extracts each statistical result the paper's own text reports (a *t*-test, a correlation, a regression coefficient) and checks whether that exact value appears anywhere in what the executed code actually printed (`match_reported_output()`). This is the closest this run comes to asking not just "does the code run" but "does running it get you the paper's own numbers."

Metacheck's statistical-output extraction and matching machinery is not, in general, R-only: `reproducibility_check` also reads and STATO-tags the rendered result tables inside a `.jasp`/`.omv`/`.spv` file (JASP, jamovi, or SPSS Viewer — self-reproducible bundles that carry both the data and its analysis together, requiring no code execution at all) via `read_stat_tables()`, feeding the same matching step as executed R output. Checking directly against every one of the 133 papers' own saved statistical output (802 extracted result entries in total), however, finds every single one came from executed R code — none from a JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer file. So the papers below happen to be entirely R-based, but this is a fact about which papers in this specific corpus had a matchable non-R statistical-output file (apparently none), not a restriction the matching step itself imposes; `reproducibility_check`'s own code-*execution* phase is separately, and by explicit design, restricted to `language == "R"` files (`inst/modules/reproducibility_check.R`), so a SAS, SPSS-syntax, Stata, Python, or MATLAB script is never itself run, whether or not a self-reproducible output file exists alongside it.

133 papers had at least one statistical result Metacheck could both extract from the paper's own text and attempt to match against the executed code's console output (`repro_tests_reported > 0`); across those 133 papers, 802 individual reported test statistics were checked, of which only 66 (8.2%) were matched by the code's actual output. At the paper level, the median proportion of a paper's own reported results its code reproduced was **0%**: only 1 of the 133 papers (0.8%) had its code reproduce *every* reported result it checked, 123 (92.5%) reproduced *none* of them, and the remaining 9 (6.8%) reproduced some but not all. This is the single starkest number this run produced, and — read together with the execution-outcome breakdown above — is consistent with a straightforward, largely mechanical explanation rather than a claim about the underlying research: a script has to actually run to completion and print a result before that result can be compared to the paper's text at all, and only 45.4% of scripts, and just 24.8% of papers in full, cleared that first bar in this run.

**Was this matching step itself useful, beyond confirming the headline 8% figure?** Yes, in two ways. First, of the 66 matched values, 62 (93.9%) matched at "full" confidence (every component of that reported test — the statistic, its *p*-value, its confidence interval — matched together) and only 4 (6.1%) matched "partially" (some but not all components of the same test found) — when this run's code did reproduce a result, it almost always reproduced it completely, not approximately; a partial match was the exception, not the norm. Second, the matcher records, separately from whether a value was found at all, whether an unmatched reported statistic could still be *traced* to a real, identifiable quantity in the code's output (`plausible_split`, flagged only for a test whose reported components had to be re-grouped from the paper's own text rather than read as originally written). Of the 736 reported values *not* matched, 523 (71.1%) were nonetheless flagged `plausible_split = TRUE` — meaning the value the paper reports does correspond to a real quantity the code computed somewhere, under a different grouping or a different analysis than the paper's own text suggested, rather than being absent from the output altogether. This is a genuinely useful distinction this run's matching step draws for free: "the code never produced anything resembling this number" is a materially different, more serious finding than "the code produced this number, just not packaged the way the paper's text implies it should be," and only the row-level `match_table` this appendix worked from here — not the paper-level `repro_tests_matched` count alone — can tell the two apart.

**A note on scope and what this section does not claim.** The numbers above describe whether a paper's own downloaded code, as shared, ran and reproduced its own reported results inside this specific execution environment (Docker, `ghcr.io/scienceverse/metacheck_r:latest`'s pre-installed package set, a 3,000-second per-script budget, no network access during execution). A script failing here is not necessarily evidence the paper's underlying research is wrong, or even that the code never worked — it may simply never have been intended to run outside the author's own machine, a point the `file.choose()` and multi-script "designed as an interactive pipeline" patterns above illustrate directly. Nor does this section attempt to re-diagnose *why* each of the 1,829 errored or 447 skipped scripts individually failed beyond the categories `reproducibility_check` itself records; a full per-paper qualitative review of this kind, in the same style as Appendix A.1–A.6's disagreement-by-disagreement review of `repo_check`/`data_check`/`code_check`, is listed as a further step in A.7.6 below rather than attempted here.

### A.7.5 Infrastructure failures, found and fixed during this run

Running `reproducibility_check` at corpus scale, for the first time, using Metacheck's new `workers`-based concurrency feature, surfaced five defects in Metacheck itself — none related to a paper's own code or data, all specific to the mechanics of running many papers' Docker containers concurrently, checkpointing their results, or (the fifth) extracting a paper's own declared dependencies from its code. All five were filed as issues against `scienceverse/metacheck`; two are confirmed fixed on the `dev` branch as of this writing (verified directly against the installed package's own source, not merely by the issue's own open/closed status), the other three are filed and not yet independently reverified.

**scienceverse/metacheck#417 — a Docker container left running after its own script's timeout fires.** `repro_run_scripts_docker()`'s per-script timeout (`processx::run(..., timeout = timeout)`) kills the host-side `docker run` CLI process when a script exceeds its budget, but this does not guarantee the container itself stops — confirmed live twice during this run: once, a `caret`/`gbm` hyperparameter grid search (490 combinations) continued running inside its container at 100% CPU for over 80 minutes after its own timeout had already fired and been correctly recorded as `outcome = "timed_out"`; a second time, a script calling `rstanarm::launch_shinystan()` (the interactive-session case named in A.7.4 above) was left running, near-idle, on a listening port after its own timeout. Both were stopped manually (`docker stop`) after being noticed via `docker ps -a`/`docker stats` from outside the run entirely — nothing in the run's own log output indicated either container was still running. **Not yet confirmed fixed.**

**scienceverse/metacheck#418 — a multi-line `deparse()` silently corrupts the generated install script for a paper with many dependencies.** `repro_install_deps_docker()` builds the container's install script with `paste0(".repro_docker_pkgs <- ", deparse(install_deps$package))` — but `deparse()` returns a **vector** of lines, not a single string, once its argument is long enough to wrap (R's own default line-width behaviour); `paste0()` silently keeps only the first line, splitting the vector literal apart mid-declaration. Confirmed live: a paper declaring 18 CRAN dependencies produced a generated `install.R` reading `.repro_docker_pkgs <- c("bayestestR", ..., "lubridate",` on one line, followed by a syntactically invalid continuation, which failed with `Error: unexpected symbol` and reported all 18 of that paper's dependencies as failed installs — not because any package itself was unavailable, but because the install script that would have installed them was never valid R in the first place. A full scan of every batch already completed at the time this bug was found identified 34 of 1,861 papers (1.8%) hit by this exact corruption signature; those 34 papers' checkpoint files were deleted and recomputed once metacheck#420 (below) was fixed and this run was restarted. **Not yet confirmed fixed** (the affected 34 papers were recomputed under the pre-fix code path avoided by deletion-and-rerun, not by an actual code fix landing on `dev`; a real fix for this specific defect remains open as of this writing).

**scienceverse/metacheck#419 — `collect_module_tables()` always returns an empty result.** `capture_module_tables()` (the function `results_dir` uses to write each paper's per-paper `.rds` checkpoint) saves each module's output into an **unnamed** list; `collect_module_tables()` (the function meant to read those checkpoints back and reassemble them) looks each module up **by name** — so every lookup silently misses, and `collect_module_tables()` returns an empty data frame no matter how many papers were genuinely saved, with no warning that anything went wrong. This defeated `results_dir`'s entire stated purpose (a resumable, inspectable per-paper checkpoint) the first time this run's own wrapper script tried to use it to reconstruct a batch interrupted partway through. **Confirmed fixed** on `dev` (commit `033294d`, "Fix capture_module_tables() saving modules unnamed"): `capture_module_tables()` now names its saved list by each module's own `$module` field, with a positional fallback for a missing or duplicate name. This project's own run script does not depend on the fix either way going forward, since it was changed to read each paper's saved `.rds` file directly (`modules[[1]]`, positionally) rather than through `collect_module_tables()`, once the defect was found live and a fix could not be waited for mid-run.

**scienceverse/metacheck#420 — `.reproducibility_check_batch()` can hang indefinitely, silently dropping the last papers in the queue.** Confirmed live: a run processing 1,861 papers at `workers = 5` reached 1,859 of 1,861 with no error, no further log output, all five worker processes idle (alive but with frozen CPU time across repeated checks 10+ minutes apart), and zero Docker containers running — yet the function never returned. The two remaining papers had no `-> starting` log line at all; `launch()` had simply never been called for them. The maintainer's own diagnosis and fix (reported back to this project directly, not independently re-derived here) was a `callr` pipe deadlock: `callr::r_bg()`'s default stdout/stderr capture uses a pipe, and once a worker produces enough output to fill that pipe's buffer with nothing reading it, the worker blocks trying to write, indefinitely, with no error surfaced anywhere. **Confirmed fixed** on `dev` (commit `85c8c87`, "Fix .reproducibility_check_batch() hang from callr pipe deadlock"): each worker's stdout/stderr is now redirected to a file rather than a pipe, and read back from that file rather than via `p$read_all_error()`'s pipe-based accessor. The stalled run was killed and restarted after this fix landed; `results_dir`'s per-paper checkpoints meant the restart correctly skipped the 1,859 already-completed papers (reported live: `"resuming -- 1859/1861 paper(s) already saved in results_dir from an earlier interrupted run"`) and completed only the two genuinely outstanding papers.

**scienceverse/metacheck#421 — dependency extraction can mistake a paper's own install-loop variable name for a package name.** Found while extracting and summarising which packages failed to install across this run (A.7.4 above): a paper's own dependency-installing boilerplate commonly assigns its package list to a variable and iterates it in a loop (e.g. `list.packages <- c(...)`, then `for (pkg in list.packages) install.packages(pkg)`); in six confirmed cases, the extractor captured a bare loop-variable identifier itself — `x`, `package`, `dependencies`, `not_installed`, `arma`, `packages.toinstall` (plus, in a seventh and eighth case, `list.packages` and `req.lib` themselves, the variable names from the concrete example quoted in A.7.4) — as if it were a literal package name to install, rather than recognising it as a variable reference whose value static analysis cannot generally resolve. Each of these eight tokens was confirmed absent from CRAN entirely (`"x" %in% rownames(available.packages())`, and equivalently for the other seven, all `FALSE`) and, on direct inspection of the originating paper's own repository code, traced to exactly this pattern. **Not yet confirmed fixed.**

**Sixteen further papers recovered by a targeted rerun.** Independently of #420's queue-loss bug, 16 of the 1,861 papers (0.9%) received a synthetic `traffic_light = "error"` stand-in result during the main run rather than a genuine check, due to either a `callr` subprocess itself crashing (`"could not start R, exited with non-zero status, has crashed or was killed"`, 14 papers) or a transient Docker Desktop outage on the host machine (`"Docker does not appear to be running"`, 2 papers) — infrastructure noise, not a property of any of these 16 papers' own code. All 16 were identified by grepping the run's own log for this failure signature, listed explicitly in `rerun_infra_failures.R`, and rerun in a small, separate, `workers = 4` batch once the main run finished; 15 of the 16 completed with a genuine result on this second attempt and were merged into the corpus-wide combined output in place of their placeholder rows. The remaining paper (10\_1111\_2041\_210x\_13384) crashed with the identical `callr` error on *both* the original run and the 16-paper rerun; a third, solo attempt (`workers = 1`, no concurrency, `rerun_single_paper.R`) found this paper's repository contains 314 separate scripts and a 1,386-row file-materialisation plan — substantially larger than any other paper's repository encountered during this run — and was manually cancelled, still mid-dependency-install, after several minutes with no sign of proceeding to actual script execution. This paper's result in the corpus-wide combined output is explicitly recorded as `outcome = "timed_out"` with a `not_runnable_reason` naming this exact sequence of events, rather than left as an ambiguous crash placeholder or given a fabricated genuine result.

### A.7.6 Suggestions for improving `reproducibility_check`

The following suggestions are drawn directly from running the module at full corpus scale for the first time; each is grounded in a specific, confirmed observation from this run, not a general aspiration.

1. **Add a distinct outcome for "this script requires interactive input."** Both `file.choose()`-driven `read.csv()` calls and `launch_shinystan()`'s blocking Shiny server (A.7.4) currently surface as an ordinary `runtime` error or a `timeout`, indistinguishable from a genuine bug in the paper's code. A small, targeted check — recognising a short list of known-interactive calls (`file.choose()`, `menu()`, `readline()`/`readLines(file("stdin"))`, `shiny::runApp()`/`launch_shinystan()`/`plotly::orca()`-style blocking viewers) before execution, or classifying a script that produces zero stdout before timing out as `timed_out_interactive` rather than plain `timed_out` — would let a report distinguish "this code cannot run unattended by design" from "this code is simply slow," two very different findings for an author or reader trying to act on the result.
2. **Preserve the install-failure *package name and reason*, not just a count, through to the paper-level summary table.** `repro_install_deps_docker()`'s own return value already carries both which package failed and a classified reason (a version incompatibility, a missing system library, a compilation failure, genuine unavailability — see `.repro_classify_install_message()`), but this run's corpus-wide saved `summary_table$repro_deps` retains only a per-paper count. This project could still recover the *names* by re-parsing each paper's free-text `report` field (A.7.4 above), but not the classified *reason* — a structured `summary_table` column (e.g. `repro_deps_packages`, `repro_deps_by_category`) would make both available directly, for every paper, without a second extraction pass against unstructured text. This would also let a report distinguish "this paper's code cannot run today because CRAN removed a dependency it used" (an ecosystem-drift problem, not a fault of the paper) from "this paper's code cannot run because it needs a system library this environment does not provide, e.g. the GDAL/GEOS/PROJ stack behind `sf`/`rgdal`/`rgeos`/`maptools`, together the largest single cluster of failed installs this run found" (an environment gap Metacheck could plausibly close by extending its own Docker image).
3. **Auto-stop a script's container on timeout (metacheck#417), not just the host CLI process.** As documented in A.7.5, a timed-out script's container can keep running, and consuming real host resources, for a long time after the timeout is reported — capturing the container's own ID (e.g. via a fixed `docker run --name`) and explicitly `docker stop`/`docker kill`ing it when `processx::run()` reports a timeout would close this gap directly, and would have prevented two of the interventions this run's own operator had to make manually.
4. **Guard every `paste0(prefix, deparse(x))` call site against multi-line `deparse()` output** (metacheck#418), not only the one instance this run happened to trigger — `deparse1()` (base R, available since R 4.0) exists specifically to always return a single string regardless of length, and is a direct drop-in replacement everywhere this pattern appears.
5. **Retry a `callr` subprocess crash once before recording it as the paper's result**, at least for `.reproducibility_check_batch()`'s `workers > 1` path. 9 of this run's 16 infrastructure failures (56.3%) were a bare `callr` subprocess crash with no more specific diagnosis available (`"could not start R, exited with non-zero status, has crashed or was killed"`) — a category that, by its own error text, cannot currently be distinguished from a genuine, reproducible crash in the paper's own code (as the twice-crashed paper in A.7.5 turned out to be) without a human manually re-running it, as this project had to do for all 16.
6. **Add a repository size/complexity gate to `reproducibility_check` specifically**, analogous to `download_repo_files()`'s existing `max_files_per_repo`/`max_file_size`/`max_download_size` caps (Appendix A.4). The one paper this run could not complete even alone (A.7.5) has a 314-script repository — nothing in `reproducibility_check` currently flags or specially handles a repository at this scale before attempting a full materialise-install-execute cycle on it, the same category of gap A.4 closed for `data_check`/`code_check`'s own download step.
7. **Make a stalled `workers > 1` run detectable from its own log**, independent of the underlying cause. Diagnosing metacheck#420 required inspecting Docker container state and OS-level process CPU time from outside R entirely, since the run's own console output gave no indication anything was wrong — it simply stopped producing lines. A lightweight, periodic "N papers still running, M queued, last completion Ts ago" heartbet message, or a caller-configurable overall wall-clock ceiling independent of any individual script's own timeout, would have made this failure mode visible from the log alone.
8. **Recognise a bare variable identifier passed to `install.packages()` as unresolvable, rather than as a literal package name** (metacheck#421). A static extractor cannot generally know a variable's runtime value, so a call like `install.packages(pkg)` inside `for (pkg in list.packages) ...` should either be skipped entirely, or resolved only when the iterated variable (`list.packages` in this example) is itself assigned a literal character vector earlier in the same file — the case in every one of this run's eight confirmed instances of this defect (A.7.5).
9. **Give `repro_install_deps_docker()` the same CRAN Archive retry `repro_install_deps()` (the `sandbox = "process"` backend) already has.** Confirmed directly against the Docker backend's own source: `repro_install_deps_docker()`'s `via_archive` field is hard-coded `FALSE` for every install attempt, with an explicit comment noting the process backend's Archive-retry-on-failure logic "is not duplicated here."
