A package whose current CRAN release fails to install (a build error, an R-version incompatibility) but whose last-published Archive version would install cleanly is therefore never given that chance under `sandbox = "docker"` specifically — the safer, actually-isolated backend this project used for exactly that reason (A.7.1) — even though the less-isolated `sandbox = "process"` backend would have tried. Checking each of the 70 one-off failed packages directly against live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (`https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/<pkg>/`, without running any paper's code) quantifies the upper bound this fix could plausibly reach: 21 (30.0%) are on live CRAN today, so their failure was for some other reason entirely, not archiving; 24 (34.3%) have no trace on CRAN at all, live or archived (a GitHub-only package, a Bioconductor package this check did not look for in the right place, or a name this appendix could not otherwise verify); and **25 (35.7%) are absent from live CRAN but do have a version sitting in the Archive** — exactly the set an Archive retry could plausibly recover, though a successful Archive fetch is not a guarantee of a successful install (the archived version could itself fail to compile, or need a system library this image still lacks), so 25 is an upper bound on what this specific fix could help with, not a prediction of how many would actually then install.
10. **Extend the full-corpus, disagreement-by-disagreement qualitative review method of Appendices A.1–A.6 to `reproducibility_check`'s own output.** This appendix reports the *rate* and *category* of non-reproducibility across the corpus, but — unlike Appendices A.1–A.6's per-disagreement review of `repo_check`/`data_check`/`code_check` — does not individually verify a sample of the 1,829 errored or 447 skipped-input scripts against their own paper's repository the way, for instance, A.3's five-check validation individually read 100+ real files. A systematic sample of `runtime`-classified failures in particular (65.4% of all errors, and the category this appendix could say the least about, since it is Metacheck's own catch-all for "every other kind of R error") would likely surface further mechanically fixable causes, in the same style A.1–A.6 already found for `repo_check`/`data_check`/`code_check`.

## A.8 Three further reliability fixes to compressed-archive handling, and their effect on `data_archive`/`code_archived`/`code_download`

An eighth round of work returned to a structural limitation named repeatedly in earlier appendices but never itself directly fixed: `zip_peek()`'s inability to read a zip's contents without downloading it on Dryad and Figshare, both of which redirect a file's download URL to Amazon S3. Diagnosing and fixing this surfaced two further, closely related defects in the same download path, and reprocessing every paper the three fixes together could plausibly affect closed most, but not all, of the remaining `code_download` disagreement this comparison's own numbers above already reflect.

**`zip_peek()` failing on S3-backed hosts (scienceverse/metacheck#424).** `zip_peek()` reads a remote zip's table of contents with two requests: a `HEAD` to learn the file's total size, then a byte-range `GET` for the tail bytes holding the archive's central directory. Amazon S3 — the storage backend both Dryad's and Figshare's own download URLs redirect to — answers the size-only `HEAD` request with 403 but answers the byte-range `GET` normally (confirmed live: a `HEAD` against a real Dryad-hosted file returned 403, while a `Range: bytes=0-100` `GET` against the identical URL returned 206 with the file's true total size in its own `content-range` header). Because `.http_range_tail()`, the function `zip_peek()` calls to fetch the tail bytes, only sends its range request once `HEAD`'s size is known, a `HEAD` failure meant the byte-range request was never sent at all — not just for Dryad and Figshare but, confirmed the same way, for Harvard's Dataverse installation, another host redirecting to S3. Fix: fall back to a suffix range request (`Range: bytes=-<n>`) when `HEAD` fails, reading the total size from that response's own `content-range` header instead. Confirmed live before and after against nine archives sampled from this corpus (three each on Dryad, Figshare, and Zenodo): all six Dryad/Figshare archives returned `NULL` from `zip_peek()` before the fix and a correct, complete listing after it, while the three Zenodo archives (not S3-backed, and so unaffected by the underlying bug) listed correctly both times.

**`zip_peek()` never persisting its result across a restart (scienceverse/metacheck#427).** A separate, longstanding defect (`repo_info_cache()`) already exists specifically to persist a repository's *listing* (which files it has) to disk, since restarting an interrupted corpus run otherwise re-pays every repository's listing cost from scratch — a real problem previously severe enough to exhaust Dryad's own daily request quota (see that fix's own code comment, confirmed live 2026-09-08: 11 restarts of one 50-paper batch cost 440+ re-listing requests against a workload that genuinely needed a handful). `zip_peek()`'s own result — a zip's *contents*, a separate cost from the repository listing above it — had no equivalent: it was cached only in memory, for the life of one R process, so the same restart pattern silently re-peeked every zip already peeked, and `repo_check` and `data_check` each peeked the same zip independently (as two separate R processes in this project's own pipeline), doubling the cost again. Confirmed directly during this project's own corpus rerun (below): before this fix, four consecutive restarts each re-hit the same Dryad rate limit at the same early batch, at increasingly long waits (24.5, then 21.5, then 16 minutes remaining); after it, a restart at the same point in the run loaded every already-completed batch from disk in under 20 seconds and progressed past the previously-stuck batch with no rate-limit wait at all. Fix: persist `zip_peek()`'s result to disk the same way `repo_info_cache()` already does for a listing, gated on the same `cache = TRUE` argument.

**A silently discarded error in `download_repo_files()`'s archive-member fetch (scienceverse/metacheck#429).** Once `repo_check`'s zip-peek expansion lists a file living inside an archive (an "archive member," carrying `archive_url`+`archive_member` rather than its own `file_url`), `download_repo_files()` fetches it via a dedicated byte-range path (`.zip_fetch_members()`/`.zip_member_fetch()`), wrapped in a bare `tryCatch(..., error = function(e) NULL)` with no logging of any kind. A transient failure at this one step — a dropped connection, a timeout, a momentary host error — left `file_location` permanently `NA` with no warning, no log entry, and no record anywhere that a download had even been attempted, indistinguishable after the fact from a member the host genuinely cannot serve. This surfaced directly in this project's own corpus rerun: after #424 above let `repo_check`/`data_check` correctly list many more Dryad/Zenodo archive members than before, 24 papers whose code repository had previously never been detected at all (`mc_code_archived` `FALSE`) newly showed `mc_code_archived` `TRUE` but `mc_code_download` still `FALSE` — the code files were now correctly found, but never downloaded. Tracing one case in full (a small `.R` file inside a Dryad-hosted zip) confirmed the underlying fetch mechanism worked perfectly when called directly, with the paper's own exact saved row data and arguments, ruling out a logic bug; the corpus run's own 17,661-line warning log had no entry at all for this archive, this paper, or any of the other 23, confirming the failure really was silently discarded rather than merely unlogged elsewhere. Fix: record the specific error `.zip_fetch_members()` raises, the same way the ordinary `file_url` download path a few lines below already does, rather than discarding it.

**Reprocessing the 24 code-download regressions.** All 24 papers' `code_check` output was rerun against `dev` after #429's fix (`code_check` alone — `repo_check`'s listing and `data_check`'s own downloads were unaffected, confirmed directly: `mc_data_download` was already correctly `TRUE` for the papers where a data download was expected). 13 of 24 resolved immediately. The remaining 11 were rerun a second time with `skip_on_api_limit` set `FALSE` for this small, targeted rerun (unlike the corpus-wide default `TRUE`, whose own rationale — never blocking an unattended, hours-long, 1,861-paper run on a host's quota reset — does not apply to an 11-paper rerun, and, confirmed directly, was itself the reason these 11 still failed: their Dryad archive fetch had landed during a rate-limit window and been silently skipped rather than waited out, and waiting the quoted remaining time fetched the exact right file on the first attempt); 4 more resolved. The final 7 each printed a `download_repo_files()` retry-exhaustion message (`Failed to perform HTTP request`, `Re-run to retry: cached files are reused, only the missing files are fetched`) that — a `message()`/`cat()` call, not a `warning()` — this project's own rerun script's `warning =` handler could not catch or log, a message-routing gap distinct from #429's own fix and not itself corrected here; rerunning those 7 a third time, as the message itself instructed, resolved all 7. Every one of the original 24 papers now downloads successfully.

**Corpus-wide effect.** With these three fixes installed and the full 1,861-paper corpus rerun, sensitivity, specificity, and the number of papers newly entering each comparison (a repository or file that previously could not be evaluated at all now can be) all moved together in the direction these fixes targeted. `code_archived` agreement rose from 84.5% to `r pct1(results$code_archived$pct_agree/100)`% (sensitivity 60.1% to `r pct1(results$code_archived$sensitivity)`%), `any_readme` from 69.8% to `r pct1(results$any_readme$pct_agree/100)`% (sensitivity 59.6% to `r pct1(results$any_readme$sensitivity)`%), and `data_availability` from 83.3% to `r pct1(results$data_availability$pct_agree/100)`%. `code_download`'s own comparable count grew from 342 to `r results$code_download$n_both_coded` papers (50 papers whose code could not previously be evaluated for a download outcome at all — because it had never been detected as archived in the first place — now can be), and agreement across that larger, harder set held at `r pct1(results$code_download$pct_agree/100)`% (`r results$code_download$n_disagree` disagreement remaining, down from 24 at the point these three fixes began). `zip_not_peeked` — the disagreement cause tracing directly to #424's own limitation — dropped to 0 as a recorded cause across every construct in this comparison's disagreement-cause categorization. The "compressed archive never opened" category among `data_archive`'s remaining under-coded papers (Appendix's own `data_archive_uncoded_papers.RData` analysis) fell from 70 papers to 12; the remainder now trace to distinct, already-documented causes (a code-only or documentation-only repository, a non-tabular file format `data_check` does not classify as data, or an image/GIS/3D file). Every previously-recorded disagreement in the corpus was re-reviewed the same way as every earlier round: 1,070 of 1,174 prior verdicts carried forward unmodified, because their underlying (paper, column, Cooper value, Metacheck value) triple was unchanged; every disagreement whose Metacheck-derived value changed, or which was newly surfaced, was reviewed from scratch (43 rows immediately after the corpus rerun above; 19 once the 24 papers' `mc_code_download` values were updated by the reprocessing described above and the comparison data rebuilt a second time) against the same evidence-source rule used throughout this manuscript (repository file listing and `repo_metadata` for `data_license`/`code_archived`/`any_readme`/`code_download`, the paper's own text for `data_availability`/`data_archive`). Every disagreement in the corpus — `r nrow(review)` of `r nrow(review)` — again carries a verdict.

## A.9 A full, paper-by-paper review of every "unsupported repository, not detected" disagreement, and a full recheck of Appendix A.6's original categorization

```{r}
#| label: a9-recheck-230-setup

# Both ID lists below are a fixed historical snapshot from when this
# review was originally conducted, not a query against the live
# corpus -- deliberately, since the review itself (which DOI resolved,
# which platform was confirmed supported, which specific defect was
# diagnosed) is a one-time, dated piece of evidence, the same way
# Appendix A.1-A.6's defect narratives are. Since then, further fixes
# elsewhere in this project have corrected several of these exact
# papers' repo_check results, which removes them from
# repo_not_detected_categorization.csv entirely (a paper no longer
# showing a "repository not detected" disagreement has nothing left to
# categorize) -- confirmed directly: every one of this chunk's
# hardcoded ids now missing from the current CSV has
# mc_data_availability == TRUE, i.e. repo_check now finds a repository
# for it. Both tables below are filtered to the ids still present in
# the current CSV, so they render only real rows rather than blank ones
# for an id the CSV no longer carries; the prose states both counts
# (as originally reviewed, and as still present) rather than silently
# reporting only one.
a9_full <- read.csv("code/03_comparing_results/repo_not_detected_categorization.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
a9_full <- a9_full[!duplicated(a9_full$article_id), ]
a9_corrected_ids <- c(
  "10_1111_2041_210x_12894","10_1111_1365_2664_13806","10_1111_1365_2664_13077",
  "10_1111_2041_210x_13175","10_1111_2041_210x_13308","10_1111_1365_2435_14709",
  "10_1111_1365_2656_13910","10_1111_1365_2435_14241","10_1111_1365_2435_13955"
)
n_230_recheck_corrected <- length(a9_corrected_ids)
n_230_recheck_corrected_still_present <- sum(a9_corrected_ids %in% a9_full$article_id)
n_230_recheck_flagged <- 21L

# a9_cats: the 40-paper "not yet individually checked" set this section's
# opening paragraph and Table 2 both need -- built here, ahead of any
# prose in this section, so the inline `r nrow(a9_cats)` expressions
# below have a defined object to read at render time.
a9_new_ids <- c(
  "10_1111_1365_2664_13709","10_1002_pan3_10149","10_1111_1365_2745_12930",
  "10_1002_pan3_10307","10_1111_1365_2745_13067","10_1111_1365_2435_14226",
  "10_1002_2688_8319_12315","10_1111_1365_2745_14315","10_1111_2041_210x_14453",
  "10_1111_1365_2745_13529","10_1002_pan3_10743","10_1111_1365_2664_12991",
  "10_1002_2688_8319_12241","10_1111_1365_2745_13517","10_1111_1365_2435_13192",
  "10_1111_1365_2435_14550","10_1002_pan3_10677","10_1111_1365_2664_13065",
  "10_1111_1365_2745_13154","10_1111_1365_2745_12749","10_1111_1365_2435_14477",
  "10_1111_1365_2656_13970","10_1111_1365_2664_13892","10_1111_2041_210x_13110",
  "10_1111_1365_2745_14252","10_1111_1365_2664_14700","10_1111_1365_2656_13918",
  "10_1111_2041_210x_13463","10_1111_1365_2435_13550","10_1111_1365_2435_12874",
  "10_1111_1365_2664_14787","10_1111_1365_2656_14227","10_1111_1365_2745_13324",
  "10_1111_1365_2656_13272","10_1111_1365_2435_13791","10_1111_1365_2745_13849",
  "10_1111_1365_2435_14514","10_1111_1365_2435_13936","10_1111_1365_2664_13845",
  "10_1111_1365_2664_14229"
)
n_a9_new_ids_original <- length(a9_new_ids)
a9_cats <- a9_full[a9_full$article_id %in% a9_new_ids, ]
a9_cats <- a9_cats[match(a9_new_ids[a9_new_ids %in% a9_full$article_id], a9_cats$article_id), c("article_id", "category", "comment")]
names(a9_cats) <- c("Paper", "Category", "Evidence and verification")

# flextable already escapes LaTeX-special characters in cell text on its
# own (confirmed: "_" in these same free-text columns already renders
# correctly elsewhere in this document without any manual escaping) --
# manually escaping here as well double-escapes it. The one real problem
# case is a literal "\b" (a regex word-boundary, in free text describing
# Metacheck's own source code) that flextable's LaTeX writer does not
# treat as needing escaping; neutralise just that by inserting a
# zero-width separator so it can never be read as a control sequence,
# without touching any other character flextable already handles.
.break_stray_backslash <- function(x) gsub("\\\\", "\\\\ ", x)
a9_cats$`Evidence and verification` <- .break_stray_backslash(a9_cats$`Evidence and verification`)
```

Appendix A.6 categorized every "repository not detected" disagreement in the corpus, but `r n_a9_new_ids_original` of the `r n_unsupported_repo_and_mc_missed` papers whose only Cooper-coded `data_archive` label(s) fell outside Metacheck's supported-platform categories, and for which `repo_check` consequently found no repository at all, had not yet been individually checked one at a time when an earlier version of this manuscript's main text was written. This appendix documents that remaining review in full: each paper's own extracted data-availability text, the specific DOI or URL cited, whether it was live-verified to resolve, whether the cited platform is genuinely supported by Metacheck (checked directly against the vendored source in `code/data/reproducibility_check/vendor/metacheck/R/`, not inferred from this manuscript's own earlier prose, which had itself gone stale for at least one platform -- see below), and the final category assigned. All `r n_a9_new_ids_original` papers received a verdict at the time of this review; `r n_a9_new_ids_original - nrow(a9_cats)` have since had their underlying `repo_check` defect fixed by later work elsewhere in this project and no longer appear in the live disagreement set at all (confirmed: `repo_check` now finds a repository for every one of them), so Table 2 below shows the `r nrow(a9_cats)` that remain.

This review also surfaced a further risk worth checking directly rather than assuming away: Appendix A.6's original 230-row categorization was itself produced before the platform-support defects this review found (the stale 4TU/DANS assumptions, an incomplete dedicated-platform list, a missing DSpace-legacy host count), so any of those original 230 rows that happened to cite one of these same platforms could be mislabeled the same way. Rather than only check the platforms these specific bugs touch, every one of the original 230 rows was rechecked from scratch: each paper's own text was re-extracted directly from the corpus (paragraph-grouped, not sentence-truncated, avoiding the extraction bug documented earlier in this manuscript), every DOI and URL in that text was identified, and each one's host was checked directly against Metacheck's current supported-platform functions -- not against what an earlier comment claimed was or was not supported.

Of the 230, `r n_230_recheck_flagged` candidate citations resolved to a host now confirmed supported despite the row's original `UNSUPPORTED_REPO` label; after excluding false positives (a truncated GitHub URL with no repository path, a citation that names a genuinely unrelated, unsupported host despite superficially matching a regex), `r n_230_recheck_corrected` rows were corrected to `SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_BUG` or `SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_MISSED` at the time of this review. The corrected rows span three recurring patterns: a citation to a genuinely supported host that `repo_check` simply never queried (Dataverse, DataOne/KNB, Zenodo, standard-format Figshare), a supported platform cited via a URL format its matcher does not parse (a Figshare private share-link or collection URL), and a supported platform cited via a non-standard DOI prefix its prefix-matching does not recognise (an alternate Dryad EZID prefix, a non-standard Figshare prefix). None of the corrected rows involve a platform Metacheck genuinely cannot reach at all -- every correction is a detection defect on an already-supported platform, consistent with the pattern the original 40-paper review above found. `r n_230_recheck_corrected - n_230_recheck_corrected_still_present` of these `r n_230_recheck_corrected` papers have since had their underlying defect fixed by later work elsewhere in this project (the same `repo_check`-now-finds-it pattern as above) and no longer appear in the live disagreement set; Table 3 below shows the `r n_230_recheck_corrected_still_present` still remaining in it, with the full original set described narratively here regardless.

```{r}
#| label: a9-corrected-230-table
#| tbl-cap: "Table 3. The rows from Appendix A.6's original 230-paper categorization corrected on full recheck, from `UNSUPPORTED_REPO` to a supported-platform category, still present in the current disagreement set."

a9_corrected_ids_present <- a9_corrected_ids[a9_corrected_ids %in% a9_full$article_id]
a9_corr_tab <- a9_full[a9_full$article_id %in% a9_corrected_ids_present, c("article_id", "category", "comment")]
a9_corr_tab <- a9_corr_tab[match(a9_corrected_ids_present, a9_corr_tab$article_id), ]
names(a9_corr_tab) <- c("Paper", "Category", "Evidence and verification")
flextable::flextable(a9_corr_tab) |>
  flextable::width(1, 1.3) |> flextable::width(2, 1.1) |> flextable::width(3, 4.6) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all")
```

Two platforms cited in this set turned out to be genuinely supported by Metacheck despite `repo_check` finding nothing, each traced to a specific, distinct defect rather than a missing backend. **4TU** (`data.4tu.nl`) has dedicated support (`archive-4tu.R`), and the DOI cited (`10.4121/uuid:04b25e70-ca3e-489f-9510-36385c1a4104`) live-resolves correctly to a real 4TU record. The ID-extractor correctly pulls the UUID from the DOI, but the live 4TU API lookup queries `data.4tu.nl/v2/articles/<uuid>`, which 404s, because 4TU's own DOI redirect resolves the identical record to a different, numeric article ID that the UUID does not match. This corrects an earlier, incorrect statement elsewhere in this manuscript (Appendix A.6) that this paper's 4TU fetch failure remained unresolved and should count as `UNSUPPORTED_REPO`; it is a supported-platform bug, not an unsupported platform. **DANS EASY** is one of four separate subject-specific Dataverse installations DANS operates (archaeology/lifesciences/phys-techsciences/ssh), all sharing a single DOI prefix (`10.17026`). Metacheck's `.dataverse_host_from_doi()` resolves any DOI under this shared prefix to `archaeology.datastations.nl`, but the paper in this set cites a dataset actually hosted on `lifesciences.datastations.nl` -- a genuine Metacheck defect in DOI-to-host resolution for any DOI prefix shared across multiple Dataverse instances, not specific to DANS. A third paper cites the Knowledge Network for Biocomplexity (`knb.ecoinformatics.org`), a confirmed DataOne member node whose DOI live-resolves correctly; the specific reason `repo_check` did not detect it was not further root-caused within the scope of this review, so it is recorded as a supported-platform miss without a fully diagnosed cause, distinct from the two fully diagnosed bugs above.

```{r}
#| label: a9-full-table
#| tbl-cap: "Table 2. Full paper-by-paper review of the 40 previously-unreviewed 'unsupported repository, not detected' disagreements: cited platform, live DOI/URL resolution status, and final category."

flextable::flextable(a9_cats) |>
  flextable::width(1, 1.3) |> flextable::width(2, 1.1) |> flextable::width(3, 4.6) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all")
```

Of these `r nrow(a9_cats)` papers, `r sum(a9_cats$Category == "UNSUPPORTED_REPO")` genuinely cite an unsupported platform, `r sum(a9_cats$Category == "NCBI_GENBANK")` cite a domain-specific bioinformatics accession outside `repo_check`'s scope, `r sum(a9_cats$Category %in% c("SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_BUG", "SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_MISSED"))` cite a platform Metacheck genuinely supports but failed to detect for the reasons described above, `r sum(a9_cats$Category == "TEXT_EXTRACTION_TRUNCATED")` had no usable citation captured in the paper's extracted text at all (either empty extraction or a citation cut off before any identifier appeared), `r sum(a9_cats$Category == "NO_REPO_DATA_RESTRICTED")` explicitly withheld their data with no repository to find, and `r sum(a9_cats$Category == "SOURCE_CITATION_ERROR")` paper's own published citation pointed to an internal, non-public address rather than a reachable repository. These per-paper counts feed directly into the corpus-wide reconciling numbers reported in the main text and into Table 1's totals above.

## A.10 Full paper-by-paper detail for every Metacheck limitation identified in the full disagreement-population review

```{r}
#| label: a10-metacheck-limitations-load

# Generated directly from manual_repo_findability_audit.csv -- the same
# file the main text's Table 1 and five-cluster breakdown are computed
# from (see the full-317-audit-load chunk above). Every row here is one
# of the n_metacheck_limitation papers from that cluster; nothing below
# is hand-transcribed, so this table stays in sync with the CSV
# automatically whenever it is updated and this document is re-rendered.
a10_labels <- c(
  CLASSIFIER_EXTENSION_GAP = "File extension not in Metacheck's lookup table",
  CLASSIFIER_MISTYPED = "Recognised extension assigned to the wrong category",
  CLASSIFIER_ARCHIVE_NOT_EXPANDED = "Archive never downloaded/opened (pipeline configuration mismatch)",
  FILES_NOT_ENUMERATED = "Repository file listing did not walk into subfolders",
  SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_BUG = "Supported platform, but a specific detection defect",
  SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_CONFIG_GAP = "Supported platform family, but this host/DOI-prefix not registered",
  EXTRACTION_GAP_DOI_GARBLED = "Citation corrupted by the PDF-to-text extraction step",
  EXTRACTION_GAP_TEXT_MISSING = "No trace of the citation in the extracted text",
  STALE_CACHE_FALSE_NEGATIVE = "On-disk cache entry predates a fix or wrongly cached a failed lookup",
  PLATFORM_URL_NOT_A_SINGLE_REPO = "Citation points to an organisation/user page, not one enumerable repository"
)

a10_tab <- full_audit[full_audit$root_cause_category %in% metacheck_limitation_cats,
                       c("paper_doi", "root_cause_category", "manual_why_metacheck_misses_it")]
a10_tab$root_cause_category <- a10_labels[a10_tab$root_cause_category]
# Order by category (in the same order as the main text discusses them),
# then by DOI within each category, for a predictable reading order.
a10_tab$.order <- match(a10_tab$root_cause_category, a10_labels)
a10_tab <- a10_tab[order(a10_tab$.order, a10_tab$paper_doi), ]
a10_tab$.order <- NULL
names(a10_tab) <- c("Paper (DOI)", "Category", "Why Metacheck misses it")
a10_tab$`Why Metacheck misses it` <- .break_stray_backslash(a10_tab$`Why Metacheck misses it`)
stopifnot(nrow(a10_tab) == n_metacheck_limitation)
```

Table 4 lists every one of the `r n_metacheck_limitation` papers in the main text's "Metacheck limitation" cluster individually: its DOI, which of the nine specific defects (grouped into the three broader categories discussed in the main text) applies, and the evidence-based reasoning for that classification, generated directly from the same per-paper audit file (`manual_repo_findability_audit.csv`) the main text's numbers are computed from. Because the table is built programmatically from that file rather than transcribed by hand, it stays reconciled with the main text's counts automatically on every re-render (confirmed by the chunk above: the table's row count is checked against `n_metacheck_limitation` directly).

```{r}
#| label: a10-metacheck-limitations-table
```
